L17: ## 1. Executive Summary
L18: ## 1.1. Product Introduction
L19: Donanemab (previously LY3002813) is a humanized immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) monoclonal antibody targeting brain amyloid plaque. Extracellular deposits of amyloid beta (A\beta) are one of two pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease, along with intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau in the form of neurofibrillary tangles. Different A\beta species are defined by their size and structure and include monomers, oligomers and protofibrils, and insoluble fibrils and plaques. Accumulation of A\beta in the brain is a defining feature of the disease that precedes neurodegeneration and clinical decline. Donanemab reduces brain A\beta plaque by targeting the N-terminal, third amino acid, pyroglutamate formation (N3pG) epitope that is present in brain amyloid plaques.
L20: The applicant's proposed indication is the treatment of Alzheimer's disease in patients with either mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia stage of disease. The proposed dosing regimen is an intravenous infusion of 700 mg donanemab over approximately 30 minutes, once every four weeks for the first three doses, followed by 1400 mg every four weeks until amyloid plaque is cleared. Donanemab is available as a 350 mg/20 mL solution in a single-dose vial for intravenous infusion.
L21: Donanemab is a new molecular entity (NME) and is not marketed in any country. The proposed proprietary name is Kisunla. The original application for accelerated approval of donanemab received a Complete Response (CR) letter on January 18, 2023, because the safety database was insufficient to adequately characterize the long-term safety of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. This resubmission application seeks traditional approval and includes the results of the pivotal clinical trial (Study AACI) and is also intended to address the deficiencies outlined in the CR letter.
L22: ## 1.2. Conclusions on the Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L23: The applicant has provided substantial evidence to support approval based on two adequate and well-controlled multicenter trials (Study AACG and Study AACI).
L24: Study AACI is a large, multicenter, adequate and well-controlled study that demonstrated statistically persuasive and clinically meaningful benefits in cognition and function in subjects with Alzheimer's disease. In Study AACI, participants treated with donanemab demonstrated a statistically significant reduced clinical decline on the primary endpoint, the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS), compared to placebo, and also on the two clinical endpoints that comprise the iADRS, the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale – Cognitive
L25: Subscale 13 (ADAS-Cog 13) and the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study – instrumental Activities of Daily Living subscale (ADCS-iADL). In addition, a clinically meaningful and statistically very persuasive effect was demonstrated for the Clinical Dementia Rating – Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB). The robust, compelling, and consistent results across multiple clinical outcomes and biomarkers, and across subgroups of the population, provide strong evidence for the effectiveness of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
L26: Study AACG was a smaller Phase 2 study that also demonstrated a statistically significant reduced clinical decline on the iADRS in participants treated with donanemab compared to placebo. Despite not reaching statistical significance according to the prespecified hierarchy, the estimates of the treatment effect across secondary endpoints, including CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog 13, and ADCS-iADL, were consistent with the reduction of clinical decline observed in Study AACI and provide independent substantiation of the benefits demonstrated in that study.
L27: Brain amyloid plaque was significantly reduced in both studies and the effects on downstream biomarkers support the observations on the clinical outcome measures.
L28: ## 1.3. **Benefit-Risk Assessment**
L29: ## Benefit-Risk Integrated Assessment
L30: Donanemab is a monoclonal antibody directed against insoluble N-truncated pyroglutamate amyloid beta. The proposed indication is the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. This reviewer recommends approval based on efficacy data from two adequate and well-controlled studies that demonstrated the clinical benefit of donanemab.
L31: Alzheimer's disease is an irreversible and progressive disease that affects memory, thinking, and behavior and is ultimately fatal. After a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease dementia, the average survival is 4 to 8 years. Alzheimer's disease was the sixth leading cause of death in the United States in 2019. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, and rivastigmine) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine are approved therapies for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, but they do not target the underlying pathology of the disease and their effects are modest and short-lived. Aducanumab and lecanemab are amyloid-beta directed antibodies that received accelerated approval and traditional approval, respectively, and are indicated for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, specifically patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or mild dementia stage of disease. There remains an urgent and unmet medical need for additional effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease, and a particular need for effective therapies to delay, halt, or reverse the pathophysiological processes that ultimately lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease.
L32: The applicant is seeking traditional approval based primarily on results from Study AACI, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study in subjects with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. Subjects were required to have evidence of brain amyloid and tau pathology on PET scans. The study included a screening period of up to 7 weeks, a 76-week placebo-controlled treatment period, and an immunogenicity and safety follow-up period of 44 weeks. Subjects were randomized to placebo or donanemab treatment in a 1:1 ratio in the placebo-controlled period. The primary efficacy endpoint was change in the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) score from baseline to 76 weeks. Secondary endpoints included change from baseline in the Clinical Dementia Rating Scale – Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) and change from baseline of the two components of the iADRS: the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale – Cognitive Subscale (ADAS-Cog 13) and the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study – instrumental Activities of Daily Living subscale (ADCS-iADL) at week 76. There were two primary analysis populations based on visual and quantitative assessment of a tau PET scan: low/medium tau population and combined population of low/medium tau and high tau levels.
L33: The primary efficacy endpoint analysis, change from baseline in iADRS at Week 76, demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect in the donanemab treatment arm compared to placebo in the combined population (2.92, p&lt;0.001) and the low/medium population (3.25,
L34: p&lt;0.001). Statistically significant reduction in clinical decline in the Division's recommended endpoint, CDR-SB, was also demonstrated, with a treatment effect of -0.70 [-29%], p&lt;0.001 in the combined population. Nominal statistical significance was reached by Week 12 and was maintained through Week 76. Results were robust across sensitivity analyses. Statistically significant results favoring donanemab were observed for the multiplicity-controlled secondary endpoints ADAS-Cog 13 (-1.33 [-20%], p&lt;0.001) and ADCS-iADL (1.70 [-28%], p&lt;0.001), the two endpoints which comprise the iADRS. Donanemab treatment demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect on change from baseline in brain amyloid as measured by PET and reported as Centiloids at Week 76 (-86.4, p&lt;0.0001).
L35: It is useful to interpret treatment difference as a percent reduction rather than the absolute point difference which depends on the length of the study and the disease stage. The results of Study AACI demonstrate a reduced decline of approximately 20% to 30% on clinical endpoints in the combined population. For CDR-SB, this corresponds to a preservation of CDR-SB by approximately 5.4 months relative to placebo over the 18 months of the study. This preservation of cognitive function is clearly clinically meaningful.
L36: Study AACG is a smaller adequate and well-controlled Phase 2 study which achieved statistical significance on the primary endpoint (iADRS). Despite not reaching statistical significance according to the prespecified hierarchy, the estimates of the treatment effect at Week 76 across secondary endpoints are consistent in magnitude with the reduction of clinical decline on the same endpoints observed in Study AACI.
L37: Study AACI is a large, multicenter, adequate and well-controlled study that demonstrated statistically persuasive and clinically meaningful benefits in cognition and function in subjects with Alzheimer's disease. The effect on CDR-SB in Study AACI represents a clinically meaningful reduction of clinical decline. This finding is supported by statistically significant results for multiplicity-controlled secondary endpoints, including endpoints capturing distinct information regarding cognitive decline and function. The treatment effect is supported by the consistently favorable results across subgroups of interest defined by demographic and baseline disease characteristics. Biomarkers reflecting brain amyloid plaque load and astrocytic activation support the observations on the clinical endpoints. Study AACG is also an adequate and well-controlled study which provides independent substantiation for the findings in Study AACI and contributes to the evidence of effectiveness.

L48: ## 2. Therapeutic Context
L49: ## 2.1. Analysis of Condition
L50: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive, degenerative brain disorder that affects memory, thinking,
L51: and behavior and is the most common cause of dementia. According to a recent report (Alzheimer's Association 2024), an estimated 6.9 million Americans age 65 years and older are currently living with Alzheimer's disease dementia. The report noted that Alzheimer's disease is the fifth-leading cause of death for those age 65 years and older. Almost two-thirds of Americans with Alzheimer's disease are women. Older African Americans and Latinos are disproportionately more likely to have Alzheimer's disease than White Americans (Alzheimer's Association 2024).
L52: Alzheimer's disease exists on a continuum from pathological changes in the brain which are undetectable to the person affected, to subtle problems with memory and thinking, and ultimately, difficulties with memory, language, problem-solving, and other skills that affect an individual's ability to perform everyday activities. The disease process may begin 20 years or more before symptoms arise (Vermunt et al. 2019). Life expectancy varies depending on many factors, but after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia the average survival is 4 to 8 years (Alzheimer's Association 2023). The long duration of the disease contributes to the burden not only on the individuals with the disease, but also their families and caregivers who provide most of the patient care and are at an increased risk for emotional distress and negative mental and physical outcomes.
L53: The two pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease are extracellular deposits of A\beta, or plaques, and intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau in the form of neurofibrillary tangles. Accumulation of A\beta in the brain has been proposed to be the primary driver of the disease process and precedes the accumulation of tau pathology and neural degeneration. Consequently, therapies to inhibit A\beta production or enhance A\beta clearance have been investigated in an attempt to slow or halt the disease process. Importantly, "anti-amyloid" therapies are not a distinct class of drugs, but rather reflect many different modes of action. A careful examination of anti-A\beta therapies has revealed that for therapies targeting aggregated forms of A\beta there exists a relationship between reduction of brain amyloid plaque and reduction of clinical decline.
L54: Some anti-A\beta monoclonal antibodies, including donanemab, have been associated with the occurrence of amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) that require special attention with respect to dosing and monitoring. ARIA covers a spectrum of imaging findings detected on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) which include ARIA-edema (ARIA-E) and ARIA-hemorrhage (ARIA-H).
L55: ## 2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options
L56: Treatment goals for patients with Alzheimer's disease are often directed to maintain quality of life, treat cognitive symptoms, and manage behavioral and psychological symptoms of
L57: dementia. Approved Alzheimer's disease treatments include the cholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist memantine, and anti-amyloid beta-directed antibodies. Aducanumab and lecanemab are monoclonal antibodies directed toward aggregated forms of amyloid and are the first therapies to receive accelerated approval and traditional approval, respectively, that target the underlying pathology of the disease.
L58: There remains an urgent and unmet medical need for effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease. In addition to the general need for more effective treatments, there is a particular unmet need for effective treatments to delay, halt, or reverse the pathophysiological processes that ultimately lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease.
L59: ## 3. Regulatory Background
L60: ## 3.1. U.S. Regulatory Actions and Marketing History
L61: Donanemab is a new molecular entity (NME) and is not currently marketed in the United States for any indication.
L62: ## 3.2. Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity
L63: IND 109157 for donanemab (previously LY3002813) was opened in the United States on February 5, 2013, for [REDACTED] (b) (4) Alzheimer's disease. This summary primarily focuses on regulatory activity related to the BLA submission and resubmission for donanemab. For a summary of regulatory activity prior to the initial BLA submission for accelerated approval refer to the previous clinical efficacy review (Krudys, DARRTS 1/17/2023).
L64: - December 22, 2022 – A Type B meeting was held to discuss the applicant's justification for changing the primary analysis method from a Bayesian disease progression model (DPM) to a natural cubic splines (NCS) model for Study AACI. The Division reminded the applicant that the use of the DPM for the primary efficacy analysis had never been agreed upon with the Division. The Division communicated their concerns with the use of the NCS model and recommended additional simulations to evaluate the type 1 error. In a subsequent submission dated January 3, 2023, the applicant provided additional supporting simulations and calculations. As a post-meeting comment, the Division responded to the January 3, 2023, submission by providing further feedback on the applicant's plan to use the NCS model. The Division also reminded the applicant of the Division's reservations about the use of the iADRS as a primary efficacy measure.
- January 18, 2023 – The Division issued a CR letter because the safety database was

L76: ## 4.4. Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology

L78: ## 4.5. Clinical Pharmacology
L79: The clinical pharmacology team has concluded that the effectiveness of donanemab was supported by amyloid PET reduction, treatment-response relationships, and mechanistic support from downstream markers of Alzheimer's disease pathology (p-tau 217, p-tau 181, and GFAP).
L80: In single doses ranging from 10 to 40 mg/kg, exposures (Cmax and AUC) of donanemab exhibited a proportional increase. Upon repeated dosing with 10 mg/kg or 20 mg/kg every 4 weeks, the AUC ratio from Day 141 to Day 1 was 1.06 and 1.26, respectively, indicating minimal accumulation.
L81: The central volume of distribution is measured at 3.36 L. Donanemab undergoes degradation by proteolytic enzymes and is not expected to undergo renal elimination or metabolism by hepatic enzymes. The mean terminal half-life of donanemab is approximately 12.1 days, and its clearance is 0.0255 L/h. Age, sex, or race did not demonstrate a significant impact on the pharmacokinetics of donanemab. Although body weight and maximum ADA titer were found to influence donanemab pharmacokinetics, the resulting changes did not affect clinical efficacy. The review team concludes that no therapeutic individualization is necessary based on intrinsic and extrinsic factors such as age, race, sex, ApoE \epsilon4 genotype, baseline tau levels, renal impairment, hepatic impairment, or ADA status. For additional details, please also refer to the OCP review in DARRTS dated 01/17/2023.
L82: Postbaseline, 793 participants in the donanemab group were evaluable for treatment-emergent ADAs (TE-ADAs) during the treatment period from Study AACI. Of these subjects, TE-ADAs were detected in 693 subjects; these subjects are therefore deemed ADA+ and the ADA incidence is 693/793 (87.4%). Neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) were detected in all the ADA+ subjects (693/693; 100%). The presence of TE-ADAs affected various PK measures, such as C_{min,ss} and AUC_{ss}. Also, the presence of TE-ADAs affected amyloid plaque reduction; subjects with higher maximum ADA titer had less amyloid PET reduction compared to subjects with lower maximum ADA titer. However, the changes in amyloid PET associated with high ADA titer did not translate into changes in efficacy measured on iADRS and CDR-SB up to week 76.
L83: The review team raised concerns about the applicant's proposal to stop treatment after plaque reduction because of limitations including reliance on a 12-month off-treatment period for calculating amyloid PET re-accumulation rate, data from a small subset of subjects for calculating amyloid PET re-accumulation rate beyond 76 weeks, lack of evaluation of long-term
L84: efficacy beyond 76 weeks, and exclusion of participants continuing on donanemab despite meeting dose cessation criteria.
L85: The review noted that ApoE \epsilon4 non-carriers and heterozygotes showed nominally higher treatment benefit and lower ARIA risk compared to homozygotes. Changes in amyloid PET and plasma biomarkers (p-tau217, p-tau181, and GFAP) reflected changes in clinical efficacy. However, given the positive trends in treatment benefit and biomarkers for all subgroups, the review team recommends dosing in all ApoE \epsilon4 genotypes, but describing efficacy and safety data in this subgroup to inform benefit-risk assessment.

L97: ## 5.2. Review Strategy
L98: The purpose of this review is to evaluate whether the results of Study AACG and Study AACI provide substantial evidence of effectiveness to support the traditional approval of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Study AACG, the relatively smaller Phase 2 study, was reviewed during the original submission for accelerated approval (Krudys, DARRTS 1/17/2023) and will only be briefly summarized in this review. The clinical efficacy review for that submission recommended accelerated approval based on a finding of substantial evidence of effectiveness on a reasonably likely surrogate endpoint. The application received a Complete Response, however, because the safety database was insufficient to adequately characterize the long-term safety of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. In response to the Complete Response letter of January 18, 2023, the applicant submitted the results of the pivotal study, Study AACI. Because accelerated approval was never granted for the original submission, Study AACI is reviewed in the context of providing substantial evidence of effectiveness for traditional approval rather than simply verifying clinical benefit. This review will therefore focus on the results of Study AACI as an adequate and well-controlled large multicenter trial which can provide substantial evidence of effectiveness. The results of Study AACG will be summarized briefly in Section 6 and referenced in the integrated analysis (Section 7.3) as providing additional evidence for efficacy.
L99: This review focuses solely on clinical efficacy. This application is being reviewed separately for safety by Dr. Branagan.
L100: ## 6. Review of Relevant Individual Trials Used to Support Efficacy
L101: ## 6.1. Study AACI (I5T-MC-AACI) Assessment of Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of Donanemab in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer's Disease
L102: ## 6.1.1. Study Design
L103: ## Overview and Objective
L104: Study AACI was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of donanemab in subjects with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. The primary objective of the study was to assess the effect of donanemab versus placebo in clinical progression as assessed by the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) at 76 weeks.
L105: ## Trial Design
L106: Study AACI was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group
L107: study in subjects with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. A total of 277 centers across 8 countries enrolled subjects into the trial. The study included a screening period of up to 7 weeks, a 76-week placebo-controlled treatment period, and an immunogenicity and safety follow-up period of 44 weeks. Subjects were randomized to placebo or donanemab treatment in a 1:1 ratio in the placebo-controlled period.
L108: Subjects who completed the placebo-controlled portion of the study had the option to enter the 78-week extension phase of the study.
L109: Randomization was stratified by investigative site and tau pathology (low/medium or high). Tau PET levels at baseline were defined by visual read and quantitative SUV R according to the following:
L110: - **Low/medium tau:** SUV R \le 1.46 and a topographic deposition pattern consistent with advanced Alzheimer's disease or 1.10 \le \text{SUV R} \le 1.46 and a topographic deposition consistent with moderate Alzheimer's disease
- **High tau:** SUV R &gt; 1.46 and a topographic deposition pattern consistent with either moderate or advanced Alzheimer's disease
L111: ## Diagnostic Criteria
L112: The protocol did not specify a formal clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, but the inclusion criteria were consistent with a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia based on operationalized criteria from the 2018 National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health and the Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al. 2018). Subjects were required to have evidence of A\beta pathology by quantitative assessment on PET and evidence of a topographic tau disposition pattern consistent with Alzheimer's disease. Subjects were also required to have gradual and progressive change in memory function for at least 6 months and evidence of a mild degree of impairment on a screening cognitive assessment.
L113: ## Key Inclusion Criteria
L114: - Gradual and progressive change in memory function reported by the patient or informant for \ge 6 months
- MMSE score of 20 to \le 28
- Male or female patients age 60 to \le 85 years
- Must have a study partner who is in frequent contact with the patient (at least 10 hours per week)
- Confirmed presence of amyloid plaques on PET (\ge 37 Centiloids)
L115: 6. Confirmed presence of tau on PET

- Topographic deposition consistent with moderate Alzheimer's disease and SUV\text{R} \ge 1.10
- Topographic deposition consistent with advanced Alzheimer's disease
L116: *Reviewer Comment: The applicant did not require a formal clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia. Instead, subjects were enrolled based on Alzheimer's disease pathology and presence of clinical symptoms and objective evidence of cognitive impairment with scoring in the mild range as assessed by the MMSE. These criteria essentially operationalized the 2018 NIA-AA Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al. 2018) (A+/T+/evidence of cognitive impairment and decline in cognitive performance from baseline). Enrollment criteria for functional status were not specified, but the population would either have no functional impairment or some degree of functional impairment with only a mild range of impairment in cognition which would also be consistent with clinical staging for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia or Stages 3 and 4 Alzheimer's disease as defined in the FDA Draft Guidance for Early Alzheimer's Disease (February 2018), although it is noted that there is potential for some subjects with a greater degree of functional impairment suggesting a moderate stage of dementia to be enrolled using these criteria.*
L117: *The specific quantitative criterion for amyloid PET was selected to ensure that subjects would have an adequate amount of amyloid, the pharmacologic target, such that they would be more likely to show a benefit. This specific quantitative criterion was designed to increase the likelihood of observing an effect in the clinical trial and does not need to be replicated in labeling, other than requiring the presence of amyloid beta pathology. Likewise, the tau PET criteria were chosen to enrich the population such that subjects would be more likely to experience clinical progression during the study and do not need to be replicated in labeling. Further discussion of efficacy across the spectrum of tau is provided in Section 7.1.3.*
L118: ## Key Exclusion Criteria
L119: - Significant neurological disease affecting the central nervous system, other than Alzheimer's disease, that may affect cognition or ability to complete the study
- Current serious or unstable illnesses including cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, gastroenterologic, respiratory, endocrinologic, psychiatric, immunologic, or hematologic diseases that could interfere with study procedures
- History of clinically significant multiple or severe drug allergies, significant atopy, or severe posttreatment hypersensitivity reactions
- Screening MRI showing evidence of a significant abnormality that would suggest another potential etiology for progressive dementia
L120: - MRI demonstrating presence of ARIA-E, &gt;4 cerebral microhemorrhages, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, any macrohemorrhage, or severe white matter disease at screening
- Alanine aminotransaminase (ALT) \ge 2.5 \times the upper limit of normal (ULN), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) \ge 2.5 \times ULN, total bilirubin level (TBL) \ge 1.5 \times ULN, or alkaline phosphatase (ALP) \ge 2 ULN at screening
- Prior treatment with a passive anti-amyloid immunotherapy &lt;5 half-lives prior to randomization or active immunization against A\beta in any other study
L121: ## Dose Selection
L122: The dosing regimen was based on safety, PK, and PD results from earlier dose-ranging studies and was chosen to balance amyloid plaque reduction and occurrence of ARIA. Briefly, doses lower than 10 mg/kg (equivalent to 700 mg in a 70 kg individual) were not associated with robust amyloid plaque reduction and a single dose of 40 mg/kg (equivalent to 2800 mg in a 70 kg individual) was associated with an unacceptable risk of ARIA. Therefore, a dose of 1400 mg was chosen as the target dose. The original protocol did not include a titration period. Based on two cases of symptomatic ARIA observed early in the study, the protocol was amended to incorporate a titration schedule of 700 mg for the first 3 doses.
L123: The protocol mandated dose cessation based on meeting specific brain amyloid thresholds. The applicant argues that amyloid plaque is the only amyloid species engaged by donanemab and therefore there is no reason to continue dosing once amyloid plaque has been reduced below a certain level.
L124: *Reviewer Comment: The decision to cease dosing once amyloid plaque is reduced below a certain threshold is not unreasonable, but there is remaining uncertainty regarding the applicant's approach as there is no direct comparison to a group of subjects who had similar plaque reduction but continued dosing. Also, the threshold commonly used to denote amyloid negativity is a useful measure, but it is still possible there could be added benefit to reducing amyloid further in this patient population. Importantly, the duration of follow-up is insufficient to assess long-term consequences of dose cessation. Therefore, there remains uncertainty regarding the optimal dosing regimen for amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies once amyloid plaque has been reduced to a very low level.*
L125: ## Study Treatments
L126: IV infusions of donanemab or placebo were administered over a minimum of 30 minutes every 4 weeks for up to 72 weeks. Subjects were to receive 700 mg every 4 weeks for the first 3 doses, then 1400 mg every 4 weeks up to Week 72.
L127: ## Assignment to Treatment
L128: An interactive web response system (IWRS) was used to assign subjects to treatment groups. Subjects were randomized equally to placebo or donanemab. Randomization was stratified by investigative site and tau pathology (low/medium or high).
L129: ## Blinding
L130: Study drug was dispensed by an unblinded pharmacist or other qualified personnel at each site. All other study site staff and subjects were blinded to treatment assignment. Investigators, subjects, and study partners were not informed of results of PET scans during the double-blind portion of the trial. The protocol specified that that CDR rater should also be blinded to adverse events (AEs).
L131: ## Dose Modification/Dose Discontinuation
L132: Double-blind dose cessation of donanemab was guided by amyloid PET levels measured at Week 24, Week 52, and Week 76. Subjects treated with donanemab could switch to placebo if their amyloid level was &lt;11 Centiloids on PET at any single visit, or ≥11 to &lt;25 Centiloids on PET at 2 consecutive visits.
L133: Specific dose modification criteria for ARIA were not established. In the event of clinically significant ARIA-E or ARIA-H, the investigator could choose to suspend treatment and monitor the patient using serial MRIs. Upon resolution of ARIA-E, stabilization of ARIA-H, and resolution of any associated symptoms, the investigator could use their judgment to reinstate treatment. For subjects who developed ARIA and had dose suspension during titration, the investigator could elect to reinstate and continue dosing with 700 mg or continue with the planned titration to 1400 mg.
L134: Temporary discontinuation of treatment was also allowed if a short-term treatment with an excluded medication was necessary, secondary to hospitalization, personal or exceptional circumstance, or to evaluate the treatment impact on an uncertain AE. In the case of a systemic hypersensitivity suspicious for an anaphylactic reaction related to treatment administration, the subject was to be permanently discontinued from treatment.
L135: ## Safety Addendum
L136: A safety addendum was added to Study AACI to collect open-label safety data in up to approximately 1000 subjects with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease who had evidence of amyloid pathology. Subjects were to receive open-label donanemab at the dosing regimen described earlier. The inclusion and exclusion criteria were similar to those for the placebo-
L137: controlled period, except the tau PET criterion was removed. Subjects who did not meet the criteria for participation in the main study were allowed to screen for the addendum if screen failure was due to a non-eligible tau PET scan or non-eligible amyloid PET scan if the amyloid level was between 24.3 and 37.1 Centiloids. Clinical efficacy assessments were not collected in the safety addendum. Change in brain amyloid plaque deposition and blood-based biomarkers were included as endpoints.
L138: ## Administrative Structure
L139: An independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) was formed to monitor the study and review safety on an ongoing basis. The DMC was to consist of at least 3 members, including a physician with expertise in Alzheimer's disease and a statistician. A statistical analysis center (SAC), consisting of third-party statisticians, prepared unblinded data for the DMC.
L140: ## Procedures and Schedule
L141: The schedule of key assessments is provided in Table 2. The lead-in screening period occurred any time prior to the screening visit and was used to collect demographic data and administer the MMSE. A period of 49 days was allowed for completion of the screening visit assessments. Study visits occurred every 4 weeks for 76 weeks with follow-up visits beginning 12 weeks after the last dose.

L146: ## Concurrent Medications
L147: Treatment of Alzheimer's disease with cholinesterase inhibitors and/or memantine was allowed if the dose had been unchanged for approximately 30 days before randomization. During the study, subjects could initiate these medications or modify their doses if deemed medically necessary. Immunoglobulin therapy was not allowed during the study.
L148: ## Treatment Compliance
L149: Subjects who attended the study visit and successfully received a complete donanemab or placebo infusion were considered to be compliant. A complete infusion is one in which at least 75% of the infusion solution was given.
L150: ## Subject Completion, Discontinuation, or Withdrawal
L151: Completers were defined as subjects who completed all required phases of the study, including the last visit or the last scheduled procedure.
L152: Subjects permanently discontinued from study treatment were to remain in the study. Subjects who prematurely discontinued from the study were to return for an early discontinuation visit and follow-up visits with clinical assessments as outlined in Table 2. Reasons for discontinuation include AE, death, lost to follow-up, physician decision, progressive disease, withdrawal by subject, and withdrawal due to caregiver circumstances.
L153: ## Study Endpoints
L154: ## Primary Efficacy Endpoint
L155: The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) at Week 76. The iADRS is a simple linear combination of the ADAS-Cog 13 and ADCS-iADL and its score ranges from 0 to 144 with lower scores indicating greater disease severity. The iADRS was developed to assess function and cognition in a single measure that is more sensitive to change and treatment effects in patients at the early stages of the disease (Wessels et al. 2015).
L156: *Reviewer Comment: In the meeting minutes of the March 2, 2021, Type C Meeting, the Division stated that, "we do not agree that a statistically significant treatment effect on the iADRS, unaccompanied by a valid statistically significant treatment effect on its two components, is acceptable for use as a primary efficacy assessment. Thus, the iADRS should not be used as your primary efficacy assessment." The Division further noted that it "was not persuaded as to whether the effects of an intervention, such as donanemab, on the iADRS could be considered necessarily clinically meaningful or reflective of effects of its individual components." The Division reiterated its concerns with the use of iADRS as the primary endpoint at the December 22, 2022, Type B Meeting.*
L157: ## Secondary Clinical Endpoints
L158: ## CDR-SB
L159: The CDR-SB assesses three domains of cognition (memory, orientation, judgment/problem solving) and three domains of function (community affairs, home/hobbies, personal care) using semi-structured interviews with the patient and a reliable companion or informant. A qualified rater uses interview data and clinical judgment to assign scores for each domain ranging from none=0, questionable = 0.5, mild = 1, moderate = 2 to severe = 3. The personal care domain does not include the 0.5 score. Scores from each domain are summed to provide the CDR-SB value ranging from 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity.
L160: Clinical Review
Kevin Krudys, PhD
BLA 761248 Resubmission
Kisunla (Donanemab)
L161: *Reviewer Comment: At the March 2, 2021, Type C Meeting the Division included the following statement in a post-meeting note, "As study AACI has already been initiated with the CDR-SB as its prospectively designated primary outcome, our advice is that this approach be retained."*
L162: ## ADAS-Cog 13
L163: The ADAS-Cog is a cognitive assessment consisting of clinical ratings and cognitive tasks that was originally developed for use in clinical trials of patients with later stages of Alzheimer's disease dementia. ADAS-Cog 11 includes 11 tasks measuring disturbances of memory, language, and praxis. Many of the items of the ADAS-Cog 11 are at the measurement floor in patients with mild disease and may not show decline over the length of a typical clinical trial. Therefore, two additional tasks, delayed word recall and number cancellation, were added to create the ADAS-Cog 13 for use in this earlier disease population. The ADAS-Cog 13 includes 9 items that test performance (up to 65 points) and 4 clinician-rated items that test language and memory (up to 20 points) for a total score ranging from 0 to 85, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive impairment. The 13 items assess word recall, ability to follow commands, constructional praxis, naming, ideation praxis, orientation, word recognition, comprehension of spoken language, memory, word-finding, language ability, delayed word recall, and concentration.
L164: ## ADCS-iADL
L165: The ADCS-ADL is a rater-administered questionnaire for informants that consists of 23 items. Informants are asked whether the patient attempted each item during the past 4 weeks and to rate the patient's performance level. The iADL is a subset consisting of 17 items measuring instrumental activities of daily living (rather than basic activities of daily living) which are thought to be more sensitive at earlier stages of the disease. The iADL score ranges from 0 to 59, with lower scores indicating greater impairment.
L166: ## MMSE
L167: The MMSE is a widely used performance-based assessment of cognitive ability consisting of 11 tasks evaluating orientation, word recall, attention and calculation, language, and visuospatial functions. The scores from the 11 tests are summed to obtain a total score, which ranges from 0 to 30, with lower scores indicating greater cognitive impairment. It is often used as a screening assessment in clinical practice or as a staging instrument for trial inclusion and is also used as an efficacy assessment in clinical trials.
L168: *Reviewer Comment: These measures capture symptoms and impacts of Alzheimer's disease that are meaningful to patients and are appropriate selections for use in supporting an effect on an acceptable endpoint.*
L169: Cognitive and functional assessments were conducted with an electronic Clinical Outcome Assessment (eCOA) tablet. Testing for each subject was to be performed at approximately the same time of day on each visit. The CDR-SB and the ADCS-ADL were to be administered by the same rater. The ADAS-Cog 13 and MMSE were to be administered by a separate rater. Whenever possible, these 2 raters were to administer the same assessments to the same individual subject throughout the study.
L170: ## Biomarker Endpoints
L171: Key biomarker endpoints included the following:
L172: - Change from baseline in brain amyloid deposition through 76 weeks as measured by ^{18}\text{F}-florbetapir or ^{18}\text{F}-florbetaben PET. The amyloid PET analysis was the SUV\text{R} calculated for a composite summary region of 6 cortical regions (anterior cingulate, posterior cingulate, medial orbital frontal, lateral temporal, lateral parietal, and precuneus) with whole cerebellum as a reference region. A negative change from baseline in SUV\text{R} indicates a reduction in amyloid burden and a negative treatment difference (donanemab minus placebo) favors donanemab. SUV\text{R} values were converted to the Centiloid scale (Navitsky et al. 2018) for analysis and reporting.
- Change from baseline in brain tau deposition at 76 weeks as measured by ^{18}\text{F}-flortaucipir PET. Global tau was measured as MUBADA (Multi-block Barycentric Discriminant Analysis) SUV\text{R}. An Alzheimer's disease signature region weighted SUV\text{R} and regional tau were measured in the frontal, parietal, and posterior lateral temporal regions with a cerebellar region as the reference.
- Change from baseline in brain volumes as measured by volumetric magnetic resonance imaging (vMRI) for the following regions: bilateral hippocampal, total brain, and ventricular.
- Change from baseline in plasma levels of neurofilament light chain (NfL), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and phosphorylated tau (p-tau 181 and p-tau 217).
L173: ## Exploratory Endpoints
L174: ## *DSST*
L175: The digit symbol substitution test (DSST) is a computer-administered neuropsychological test. Images of different types of medicines are presented as symbols and numeric calendar dates are numbers. Patients are shown a legend that indicates associations between 9 medicines and 9 calendar dates. The patient is instructed to consider each empty box in relation to the date-medicine association in the legend and select the medicine associated with the empty date box
L176: from a group of images. The performance measure is the number of correct associations between date and medicine made within 120 seconds.
L177: ## *Time to Substantial Decline*
L178: Time to a clinical worsening event was defined as meeting the following criteria at 2 consecutive visits:
L179: - Any increase in CDR global score
- \ge 1 point increase in CDR-SB for subjects with MMSE at screening of 27-30 or a \ge 2 points increase for subjects with MMSE at screening of 20-26
- 5 points decrease in iADRS for subjects with MMSE at screening of 27-30 or 9 points decrease for subjects with MMSE at screening of 20-26
L180: ## *Responder Analyses*
L181: The probability of not progressing, defined as having a CDR-SB change from baseline \le 0, was calculated at each scheduled visit. Additional exploratory analyses were performed for iADRS and CDR-SB to determine whether subjects met a prespecified percentage of disease slowing at month 12 and month 18 based on the estimated placebo decline.
L182: ## **Statistical Analysis Plan**
L183: The original Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) was issued on November 1, 2021, and was amended twice, with the final version implemented on April 20, 2023, prior to unblinding of the study data.
L184: ## Definitions of Statistical Analysis Populations
L185: The following analysis populations were the key populations defined in the SAP:
L186: - Randomized – all subjects who signed the informed consent form and were randomized to study treatment
- Evaluable Efficacy – all randomized subjects with a baseline and at least one post-baseline efficacy scale
- Per-Protocol – all subjects in the Evaluable Efficacy dataset who also signed the informed consent form, had an assessment of the primary endpoint at each scheduled visit completed, had no violations of inclusion/exclusion criteria, had no instances of receiving the wrong treatment, and were not considered non-compliant with regard to
L187: ## study drug
L188: Two additional populations are critical for interpretation of the study results: the low/medium tau population and the overall population. The low/medium tau population is defined by tau PET SUV and visual read as described earlier in the review. The overall population is the combination of the low/medium tau population and the high tau population.
L189: *Reviewer Comment: This review will present the results for both the low/medium and overall populations because they were prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. For assessment of effectiveness, however, this review will focus on the overall population, as this is the relevant population with respect to the proposed indication. It is also worth noting that these two populations are not independent, as the low/medium population makes up 68% of the overall population.*
L190: ## Sample Size Determination
L191: Sample size calculations were based on the low/medium tau population. Based on the results of Study AACG, the sample size calculation assumed a standard deviation of change from baseline in iADRS at 18 months of 11.06, a treatment difference of 3.2, and a discontinuation rate of 30%. Of the approximately 1800 subjects enrolled in the study it was assumed that approximately two-thirds of the population would have low/medium tau levels. Under these assumptions, the sample size provided greater than 95% power to achieve statistical significance at a 1-sided 0.025 level.
L192: ## Interim Analyses
L193: Interim analyses for efficacy were not performed.
L194: ## Analysis Method for Primary Endpoint
L195: A Natural Cubic Spline (NCS) model with 2 degrees of freedom (NCS2) was used to assess the difference between treatment groups in iADRS at Week 76. For the NCS2 model, 2 knots were placed at the minimum and maximum observations times and 1 knot was placed at the median observation time. The baseline estimates of iADRS were restricted to be the same for the placebo and donanemab treatment groups. Study visit was treated as a continuous variable with values equal to weeks between baseline and post-baseline visits. The model included fixed effects for NCS expansion terms (2 terms), NCS basis expansion term-by-treatment interaction (2 terms), baseline age, use of AD medication at baseline (yes or no), and pooled investigator. Baseline tau category was included as a covariate in the model applied to the overall population.
L196: ## Additional Analysis Methods
L197: A number of additional analysis methods were described in the SAP. A mixed model repeated measures (MMRM) model was also used to analyze change from baseline in clinical endpoints at Week 76 with fixed effects terms for baseline score, baseline score-by-visit interaction, pooled investigator, treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, use of AD medication at baseline (yes or no), and age at baseline. Baseline tau category was included as a covariate in the model applied to the overall population. MMRM was the primary analytical approach for CDR-SB.
L198: A time progression model for repeated measures (PMRM) was used to estimate the slowing of progression of the disease, in terms of time, for the donanemab treatment group compared to the placebo group (Raket, 2022). A natural cubic spline model with internal knots at each planned visit was used to interpolate the disease progression for the placebo arm. The donanemab disease progression was described by assuming that it could be estimated by the mean disease progression of the placebo group at another time point. The assumption of proportional time slowing was tested.
L199: A Cox proportional hazard model was used for the time to substantial decline analyses. The analyses were modeled as time to first occurrence of the event adjusting for baseline age, score, and use of AD medication at baseline and stratified by pooled investigator sites.
L200: A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with progression status (yes or no) as the dependent variable with a binary distribution was used to assess the difference in probability of not progressing by treatment arm. The model included baseline score, baseline score-by-visit interaction, treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, use of AD medication at baseline, and age at baseline as fixed effects.
L201: ## Adjustments for Multiplicity
L202: Bretz's graphical approach was used to control the study-wise type I error rate for the primary and key secondary hypotheses at a 2-sided alpha level of 0.05. For the primary analysis, the initial 2-sided alpha level was set to 0.04 for the low/medium tau population and 0.01 for the overall population. See Dr. Tran's statistical review for further details.
L203: ## Subgroup Analyses
L204: Subgroup analyses for iADRS, CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog 13, ADCS-iADL, MMSE, amyloid PET, tau PET, and plasma biomarkers were planned for the following pre-defined groups:
L205: - Age group (&lt;65, 65-74, and ≥75 years)
L206: - Sex (male, female)
- Race (White, Black or African American, Asian)
- Ethnicity (Hispanic or Latino, not Hispanic or Latino)
- ApoE \epsilon4 carrier status (carrier, non-carrier)
- ApoE \epsilon4 genotype (non-carrier, heterozygous carrier, homozygous carrier)
- Clinical staging at screening (MMSE 20-26, MMSE 27-28)
- Baseline brain tau category (low/medium, high)
- Baseline tau SUV R tercile defined by screening MUBADA SUV R
- BMI (&lt;25, 25-30, \ge 30 kg/m^2)
L207: The NCS2 model was to be used to perform subgroup analyses for iADRS, CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog 13, ADCS-iADL, and MMSE. MMRM models were used to perform analyses for amyloid PET and plasma biomarker endpoints. An ANCOVA analysis was used for the tau PET endpoints.
L208: ## Protocol Amendments
L209: The original protocol was issued on January 30, 2020, and was amended 5 times (versions (a) through (e)). Protocol amendment (a) changed the dosing regimen to include titration with 700 mg for the first 3 doses due to a higher-than-expected incidence of serious ARIA-E in the first 43 treated subjects. Protocol amendment (b) in February 2021 increased the sample size and converted the study from a Phase 2 study to a Phase 3 study to confirm the results observed in Study AACG. The primary endpoint was changed from CDR-SB in the overall or low/medium tau population to iADRS in the low/medium tau population. In version (d) a long-term extension was added to the study and the CDR was allowed to be administered to the participant or study partner by telephone. The primary analysis method was changed from Bayesian Disease Progression Model to NCS in version (e) in November 2022.
L210: ## 6.1.2. Study Results
L211: ## Compliance with Good Clinical Practices
L212: The applicant attests that the study was conducted in accordance with the principles of GCP and applicable laws and regulations.
L213: ## Financial Disclosure
L214: The applicant has adequately disclosed financial interests or agreements with clinical investigators as outlined in the guidance for industry Financial Disclosures by Clinical Investigators. There were 4 investigators at 4 different sites with disclosable financial interests or arrangements, but those sites do not have the potential to influence the overall results because of the low numbers of subjects they enrolled.
L215: ## Patient Disposition
L216: A total of 8240 subjects were screened for entry into the study and 1736 were randomized. The most common reasons for screen failure were failure to meet inclusion criteria for amyloid PET (25%), tau PET (25%) or MMSE (23%). Patient disposition is summarized in Table 3. There were 9 subjects who were randomized (2 placebo, 7 donanemab) but discontinued before receiving study treatment. A total of 137 subjects (52 placebo, 85 donanemab) were not included in the evaluable efficacy population for the primary endpoint because they did not have a baseline assessment and/or at least one post-baseline iADRS assessment or were discontinued before receiving study treatment. There were 50 subject (20 placebo, 30 donanemab) missing a baseline iADRS assessment.
L217: *Reviewer Comment: The percentage of subjects with missing baseline measurements for the primary outcome assessment (3%) was relatively higher than that observed in other recent studies. It is noteworthy that the number of missing baseline measurements for CDR-SB was less than half that for iADRS, which requires two separate assessments (ADAS-Cog 13 and ADCS-ADL). Subjects with missing baseline assessments are automatically excluded from the evaluable efficacy population and represent an unfortunate loss of valuable follow-up data, especially considering that most subjects with missing baseline iADRS went on to complete the study.*
L218: There was an imbalance in the proportion of subjects discontinuing due to AEs (2.4% placebo, 5.8% donanemab) as well as a larger number of subjects in the donanemab arm who chose to withdraw from the study. There were also 12 subjects (7 donanemab, 5 placebo) who did not complete a final visit prior to data lock.
L219: Although administration of the CDR by telephone was allowed, 98% of assessments were administered in-person at study visits, with only 13 (7 placebo, 6 donanemab) CDR assessments performed remotely at the Week 76 visit.
L220: *Reviewer Comment: The inclusion of remote assessments for CDR-SB is unlikely to affect the estimation or interpretation of treatment effects.*

L224: ## Protocol Violations/Deviations
L225: Protocol deviations that had the potential to affect subject safety or efficacy endpoints were observed in 1242 (71.6%) subjects in the study (621 in the donanemab treatment arm and 622 in the placebo arm). The most common category of deviations was related to study procedure compliance (51% in the donanemab treatment arm and 48% in the placebo arm). Review of these deviations did not reveal systemic issues which would affect the interpretation of the study results. Other important protocol deviations were generally balanced between the two arms.
L226: There were 7 instances of investigational product unblinding occurring in 7 subjects (4 in the donanemab treatment arm and 3 in the placebo arm) at 5 different clinical sites. Detailed narratives describing the unblinding events did not reveal systemic issues and corrective and preventive actions were taken in response to the events.
L227: ## Table of Demographic Characteristics
L228: Table 4 contains important information regarding demographic characteristics for each arm in the randomized population. The low/medium tau and the overall populations are highlighted because they are the two key populations for the prespecified analysis plan. Demographic characteristics were balanced across the treatment arms and generally representative of the patient population except for an under-representation of African American and Hispanic patients. Overall, 72% of subjects were enrolled in the United States. Demographic characteristics were largely similar in the low/medium tau and overall populations.

L232: ## Other Baseline Characteristics (e.g., disease characteristics, important concomitant drugs)
L233: Table 5 contains a summary of key baseline disease characteristics and baseline use of concomitant Alzheimer's disease medications (i.e., cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine) for both the low/medium tau and overall populations. Disease characteristics are balanced across treatment arms and reflect a population early in the course of Alzheimer's disease. The percentage of the overall population who were ApoE \epsilon4 carriers (70%) is consistent with other studies in this population as is the proportion of subjects receiving concomitant medications for Alzheimer's disease (61%). A clinical diagnosis of MCI due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's dementia was not required for study entry and some subjects were apparently enrolled prior to diagnosis. Baseline characteristics are consistent with an operationalization of the 2018 NIA-AA Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (A+/T+/evidence of cognitive impairment and decline in cognitive performance from baseline). Overall, the mean baseline scores on the CDR-SB, MMSE, ADAS-Cog 13, and the ADCS-iADL appear to be consistent with a population with mild cognitive impairment and mild to minimal impairment, although there are a few outliers who had more marked impairment on these assessments. It is notable that there were 487 subjects (28%) whose MMSE score at the baseline visit was no longer within the range used for inclusion at screening (415 subjects with MMSE &lt;20 and 72 subjects with MMSE &gt;28 as baseline). This observation was generally balanced in proportion between the two arms and is unlikely to significantly alter the interpretation of the results.

L248: ## Treatment Compliance, Concomitant Medications, and Rescue Medication Use
L249: Compliance to treatment was based on the number of subjects receiving an infusion at a given visit. Compliance ranged from 98.2% to 100% in the donanemab treatment arm and from 99.7% to 100% in the placebo arm depending on the visit. Although compliance was high, dose modifications due to adverse events, including ARIA, meant that some subjects received fewer than the 19 planned doses. For example, the mean number of infusions in the donanemab treatment arm was 14.6, compared with 16.3 in the placebo arm. A total of 42.2% of subjects in the donanemab treatment arm and 54.9% in the placebo arm received \ge 19 doses.
L250: In the donanemab treatment arm, the dose could have been reduced to 0 mg based on amyloid PET results at Weeks 24, 52, and 76 as described earlier. Of the subjects in the donanemab treatment arm who had dosing records at Week 28 (the first donanemab administration after the Week 24 PET results), 16% were receiving 0 mg. By Weeks 56 and 78, the percentage of subjects in the donanemab treatment arm with dosing records receiving 0 mg was 46% and 69%, respectively. At Week 78 (the first dosing period in the long-term extension), a total of 29% of subjects randomized to the donanemab arm were still receiving 1400 mg.
L251: Overall, 10% of study participants started a new concomitant Alzheimer's disease medication at some point during the study (12% in the placebo arm and 8% in the donanemab arm) and 4.4% (5.7% in the placebo arm and 3.2% in the donanemab arm) changed the dose of an existing Alzheimer's disease medication. The relatively higher proportion of subjects in the placebo arm starting a new concomitant medication could potentially make it more difficult to demonstrate a treatment effect in the study.
L252: ## Efficacy Results – Primary Endpoint
L253: The donanemab treatment arm demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect on the primary efficacy endpoint, change from baseline in iADRS at Week 76, compared to placebo in both the low/medium tau population (3.25 [-35.1%], p&lt;0.001) and the overall population (2.92 [-22.3%], p&lt;0.001) (Table 8). Separation from placebo was detected by Week 12, which was nominally statistically significant, and was maintained through Week 76 (Figure 1). MMRM analysis of the primary endpoint provided similar estimates of the treatment effect in the low/medium tau (3.80 [-39.6%], p&lt;0.001) and overall (3.03 [-22.9%], p&lt;0.001) populations.

L262: ***p&lt;0.001
L263: To address the potential effect of functional unblinding due to ARIA or infusion reactions, the applicant compared the results of the primary analysis to results using a reduced dataset in which all assessments after occurrence of ARIA-E or infusion reaction were excluded. The results were similar and thus do not suggest a systematic bias due to functional unblinding. It is important to reiterate that steps were taken in the protocol to minimize functional unblinding, specifically blinding of the rater to adverse events. Also, ARIA and infusion reactions occurred in the placebo arm, suggesting that investigators could not, with complete accuracy, know the subject's treatment group based on occurrence of such an event.
L264: Several sensitivity analyses, including ones requested by the statistical reviewer, demonstrated that the statistically significant results were robust to different modeling assumptions. See Dr. Tran's statistical review for more information.
L265: The treatment effect on the primary endpoint was contextualized in terms of time saved using PMRM. Donanemab treatment resulted in a statistically significant estimate of time saved of 4.4 (1.87, 6.85) months (p&lt;0.001) in the low/medium tau population and 1.4 (0.46, 2.3) months (p=0.004) in the overall population over the 18-month treatment period. Proportional time slowing was assumed in the overall population but not the low/medium tau population.

L310: ## Efficacy Results – Pharmacodynamic Endpoints
L311: ## Amyloid PET
L312: Donanemab treatment demonstrated a statistically significant effect on change from baseline in brain amyloid plaque as measured by PET and reported as Centiloids at Week 76 in the low/medium tau population (-88.2, p&lt;0.0001) and the overall population (-86.4, p&lt;0.0001) (Table 12). The results indicate a time-dependent relationship (Figure 7). In the donanemab treatment arm, 29.7% (226/761), 66.1% (443/670), and 76.4% (469/614) of subjects who had an amyloid PET scan had Centiloid levels less than 24.1 at Weeks 24, 52, and 76, respectively. There were 2 subjects (0.3%) in the placebo arm with Centiloid levels less than 24.1 at Week 76. At Weeks 24, 52, and 76, the proportion of participants in the donanemab treatment arm who met dose stopping criteria based on amyloid PET results was 17%, 42%, and 60%, respectively.

L323: ## vMRI
L324: Donanemab treatment was associated with a decrease in whole brain volume and an increase in ventricular volume at Week 76 (Table 14). Similar changes have been observed with other monoclonal antibodies targeting aggregated brain amyloid. Although it is possible that the findings could represent atrophy, given the favorable results on clinical endpoints observed in Study AACI, the clinical relevance of these changes is unclear. It is also notable that, in contrast to whole brain and ventricular volume changes, there was a trend for a reduction in volume loss in the hippocampus with donanemab treatment.

L347: ## Time to Substantial Decline
L348: Donanemab treatment reduced the risk of progression on the CDR global score by 39% with a hazard ratio of 0.61 (0.47, 0.80), p&lt;0.001 in the low/medium population and by 37% with a hazard ratio of 0.63 (0.51, 0.77), p&lt;0.0001 in the overall population. A total of 100 (18%) donanemab-treated subjects and 163 (28%) placebo-treated subjects had substantial decline in the CDR global score in the low/medium tau population and 186 (23%) donanemab-treated subjects and 288 (34%) placebo-treated subjects had substantial decline in the overall population.
L349: Donanemab treatment also reduced the risk of progression on the CDR-SB (\ge 1 point increase for subjects with MMSE at screening of 27-30 or \ge 2 points increase for subjects with MMSE at screening of 20-26) by 40% with a hazard ratio of 0.60 (0.47, 0.75) in the low/medium tau population and by 38% with a hazard ratio of 0.62 (0.52, 0.75) in the overall population. Similarly, the risk of progression on the iADRS (5 points decrease in iADRS for subjects with MMSE at screening of 27-30 or 9 points decrease for subjects with MMSE at screening of 20-26) was reduced with donanemab treatment by 36% with a hazard ratio of 0.64 (0.51, 0.81) in the low/medium tau population and by 30% with a hazard ratio of 0.70 (0.58, 0.84) in the overall population.
L350: ## Responder Analysis
L351: A total of 47% (42%, 51%) of donanemab-treated subjects in the low/medium tau population were non-progressors (CDR-SB change from baseline \le 0) at Week 52 compared to 29% (25%, 33%) of placebo-treated subjects (p&lt;0.00001). In the overall population, 36% (33%, 40%) of donanemab-treated subjects were non-progressors at Week 52 compared to 23% (20%, 26%) of placebo-treated subjects.
L352: ## Dose/Dose Response
L353: A dose-response relationship was not observed because only a single dosing regimen was included in the study. Greater amyloid plaque reduction was associated with higher doses of donanemab in the single- and multiple-ascending dose study (AACD). See the clinical pharmacology review for further information, including evaluation of exposure-response relationships.
L354: ## Durability of Response
L355: Statistically significant treatments effects for the primary and secondary endpoints were generally observed by the 3-month visit, and the absolute treatment difference tended to increase over time for the 18 months of the placebo-controlled portion of the study. Amyloid plaque continued to decline to levels consistent with amyloid negativity by visual read on PET imaging following dosing with donanemab. It is anticipated that with a drug that impacts the underlying disease biology that the treatment benefit will increase over time and that is, in fact, what was demonstrated in Study AACI over 76 weeks. Durability of response for a longer period of time may be addressed when data from the long-term extension portion of the study become available.
L356: ## Persistence of Effect
L357: Study AACI was not designed to address the effect of donanemab after treatment is stopped or withheld. There were a number of donanemab-treated subjects who had their dose reduced to placebo during the study based on amyloid PET results, but data from these subjects are inadequate to draw conclusions regarding persistence of effect on clinical endpoints due to the relatively short off-treatment period, the lack of an appropriate comparator group, and the fact that donanemab continues to exert a pharmacodynamic effect after dose cessation. The applicant assumed that cessation of donanemab dosing once brain amyloid on PET was reduced beyond a specific threshold would not adversely affect clinical outcomes. Although this assumption may be reasonable, there is still some uncertainty about the appropriate threshold, and the assumption was not verified by including an arm with continuous donanemab dosing. Data from the ongoing long-term extension portion of the study or from the ongoing Study AACM in preclinical Alzheimer's disease may provide insight into the persistence of effect.
L358: Using data from patients who completed active treatment based on amyloid imaging, amyloid levels began to increase with a mean rate of 2.8 Centiloids/year. Data suggest that re-accumulation of plasma markers may occur at a faster rate than amyloid plaque on PET (see Figure 9 in Dr. Nookala's clinical pharmacology review). Although re-accumulation of amyloid plaque is relatively slow at the mean level, the potential for re-initiation of donanemab based on amyloid levels remains uncertain and untested.
L359: ## 6.2. Study AACG (I5T-MC-AACG) Assessment of Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of LY3002813 in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer's Disease
L360: Study AACG, a smaller Phase 2 study, was reviewed during the original submission for accelerated approval (Krudys, DARRTS 1/17/2023) and will only be briefly summarized here.
L361: A total of 1995 participants were screened for entry into the study and 272 participants were randomized (126 placebo, 131 donanemab, 15 donanemab in combination with LY3202626). Of the 257 participants randomized to the placebo or donanemab arms, 32 participants (25%) receiving placebo and 37 participants (28%) receiving donanemab discontinued from the study. At baseline, the mean age of randomized participants was 75 years with a range of 61 to 86 years. Forty-seven percent of participants were male and 95% were white.
L362: The primary efficacy endpoint analysis of change from baseline in iADRS at Week 76 demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect in the donanemab treatment arm compared to placebo (3.2; 95% CI 0.1, 6.3; p=0.04; 32% reduction). The difference between the donanemab group and the placebo group in the change from baseline in CDR-SB at Week 76 did not reach statistical significance (-0.4; 95% CI -0.8, 0.1; p=0.14; 23% reduction). Differences between the donanemab group and the placebo group in the change from baseline at 76 weeks were 1.9 (95% CI -3.6, -0.1; 39% reduction) for ADAS-Cog 13, 1.2 (95% CI -0.8, 3.2; 23% reduction) for ADCS-iADL, and 0.6 (-0.4, 1.7) for MMSE. Donanemab treatment demonstrated a reduction in brain amyloid plaque reported as Centiloid and compared to placebo at Week 76 (placebo least square (LS) mean change from baseline 0.9; donanemab LS mean change from baseline -84.1; treatment LS mean change difference -85.1; 95% CI -92.7, -77.4).
L363: ## 7. Integrated Review of Effectiveness
L364: ## 7.1. Assessment of Efficacy Across Trials
L365: ## 7.1.1. Primary Endpoints
L366: The primary endpoint in Studies AACG and AACI was the change from baseline in iADRS at Week 76. Studies AACG and AACI shared many design characteristics and enrolled a similar patient population with early Alzheimer's disease. The main differences between the studies were: (1) AACG was a smaller Phase 2 study enrolling approximately 15% the number of subjects of Study AACI, (2) Study AACG only enrolled subjects with low/medium tau load on tau PET whereas Study AACI also allowed enrollment of subjects with high tau load, (3) both studies allowed down titration to placebo, but Study AACG included down titration to 700 mg donanemab, and (4) Study AACI included fewer protocol-mandated dosing restrictions based on ARIA. The most direct comparison for Study AACG is the low/medium tau population from
L367: ## Study AACI.
L368: A summary of the results for iADRS across the two studies is displayed in Table 17. The statistically significant result in favor of donanemab in Study AACI is consistent with the result from Study AACG. The magnitude of the effect is also remarkably consistent in the low/medium tau populations in the two studies. The smaller magnitude of the treatment effect estimate in the overall population in Study AACI provides support for the applicant's hypothesis that an earlier population with less tau pathology is more likely to respond to donanemab.

L373: ## 7.1.2. Secondary and Other Endpoints
L374: The disagreement over the choice of iADRS as the primary endpoint is mostly inconsequential because positive results were also observed for the CDR-SB and both components of the iADRS, ADAS-Cog 13 and the ADCS-iADL, which were secondary endpoints in Study AACI. These secondary endpoints encompass two acceptable approaches suggested by the Division to the applicant: (1) CDR-SB or (2) ADAS-Cog 13 and ADCS-iADL as coprimary endpoints.
L375: Results for CDR-SB in the two studies are presented in Table 18. CDR-SB was the first ranked secondary endpoint in both studies. The statistically significant results for iADRS in Study AACG, but not CDR-SB may suggest that iADRS is a more sensitive measure appropriate for smaller studies. The statistically significant results with low p-values in Study AACI for both endpoints suggest that large pivotal studies may not be sensitive to the choice of endpoint.

L395: ## 7.1.3. Subpopulations
L396: Subpopulation results for Study AACI are presented in Figure 2 and Figure 4, for iADRS and CDR-SB, respectively. With the exception of the small subgroups of Black/African American race for iADRS and Hispanic/Latino ethnicity for CDR-SB, findings are generally consistent with the overall population estimate and favor treatment with donanemab. Pooled data is not presented because Study AACI has a sufficient number of subjects to support meaningful conclusions for relevant subgroups.
L397: ## Baseline Tau Levels
L398: Further consideration of efficacy across the spectrum of baseline tau levels is relevant because tau PET imaging was used as an enrichment strategy in Studies AACG and AACI. The applicant does not propose a requirement for confirmation or quantification of tau pathology in the prescribing information despite excluding subjects with no or very low tau from the controlled
L399: portions of Studies AACG and AACI and prioritizing a low/medium tau population in the statistical analysis of Study AACI.
L400: Donanemab is an anti-amyloid antibody and, as such, does not require the presence of tau to exert its intended pharmacologic effect. The sequence of pathologic events is complex, but in general, brain amyloid accumulates before abnormal tau, and increased brain amyloid is directly associated with subsequent tau accumulation and neurodegeneration. Aggregated forms of amyloid beta can also be directly toxic to synapses and neurons. Therefore, there is no *a priori* reason to believe that a certain level of tau needs to be present for donanemab to be effective. On the contrary, current efforts, including an ongoing study with donanemab, are focused on intervening even earlier in the disease when tau levels are expected to be minimal.
L401: It is also important to note that a negative tau PET scan with flortaucipir does not preclude the presence of tau pathology. The TAUVID prescribing information notes that performance for detecting tau pathology may be lower in patients in earlier stages of the pathologic spectrum, such as patients enrolled into Study AACI. Furthermore, neuropathogenic assessment has demonstrated that most symptomatic, amyloid positive patients also have some degree of tau pathology (Serrano-Pozo et al. 2013). Therefore, the underlying pathophysiology of the disease is not anticipated to be significantly different between symptomatic amyloid positive patients with no or very low tau on PET compared to those with higher levels of tau on PET.
L402: The decision to exclude subjects with no or very low tau from Studies AACG and AACI was based on research conducted by the applicant demonstrating that subjects with nonadvanced patterns of tau deposition were less likely to exhibit disease progression as measured by CDR-SB over an 18-month period (Lu et al. 2021). Accordingly, simulations suggested substantially greater statistical power in studies enrolling subjects with more advanced tau deposition (Qian et al. 2017). Therefore, tau burden served as a prognostic biomarker to reduce the number of non-progressors enrolled in the studies, and exclusion of subjects with no or very low tau was primarily a statistical consideration to decrease the sample size and increase the ability to detect a change during the 18-month duration of the study.
L403: Although there is no clinical efficacy data in subjects with no or very low tau, there is biomarker data from a single-arm, open-label, safety addendum to Study AACI. This addendum included a cohort of subjects who failed the tau PET entry criterion for entry into the double-blind portion of the study. Compared to subjects with low/medium or high tau enrolled in Study AACI, subjects with no or very low tau had lower baseline levels of key biomarkers, consistent with their earlier disease stage. Reductions from baseline were generally similar in the two populations (Figure 9).
L404: Data suggest that the degree of tau pathology is related to symptom severity and stage of disease, and therefore, is generally associated with a greater degree of neurodegeneration
L405: (Ossenkoppele et al. 2016) Therefore, it can be reasonably expected that patients with higher tau burden have a greater extent of neurodegeneration and the potential for benefit may be more limited in this population compared to patients with low tau burden. The primary results of Study AACI in the low/medium and overall populations appear to support these expectations. Nevertheless, the prespecified subgroup analyses by baseline tau tercile (Figure 2 and Figure 4) suggest that a treatment effect was observed across the range of baseline tau levels included in Study AACI, including in subjects with high tau levels. Patients with no or very low tau burden may be more likely to benefit from anti-amyloid therapy, but due to the slower rate of their disease progression, the time needed to manifest that treatment effect may be much longer than the 18-month duration of a clinical trial such as Study AACI. The applicant also performed an analysis to explore the relationship between tau levels and efficacy by including baseline tau SUVR, baseline tau SUVR-by-visit, and baseline tau SUVR-by-treatment-by-visit interactions in the original MMRM model described in the statistical analysis plan. Greater relative treatment effects (i.e., percent slowing) were estimated with decreasing baseline tau levels over the range of tau SUVR in the study. This analysis suggests that the benefits of donanemab may be greater in patients in earlier stages of disease with lower tau burden.
L406: It is also important to note that the incidence of ARIA was similar or possibly less in subjects with no or very low tau compared to subjects with high tau (please refer to the safety review by Dr. Branagan).
L407: In conclusion, higher levels of tau on PET imaging were used as a strategy to enrich for subjects who were more likely to progress during the 18-month study. Subjects who meet criteria for Alzheimer's disease based on confirmed presence of brain amyloid and cognitive impairment have the same underlying pathophysiology of disease regardless of the tau burden. The course of the disease is also progressive for all tau levels, although a higher tau burden reflects a later stage of disease that may progress more rapidly. The pharmacodynamic effect of the drug is expected to be similar in patients who are amyloid positive, regardless of tau status, and in fact subjects with no or very low tau treated during the safety addendum showed similar reduction in amyloid plaque on PET and on other pharmacodynamic markers as those with higher tau levels. Furthermore, modeling suggests that clinical benefit may be even greater in patients with lower tau burden. Safety was similar across the spectrum of tau burden. Based on these considerations, it is reasonable to generalize the efficacy results from the population studied in Study AACI across the spectrum of tau burden, including patients with very low or no tau.
