L412: ## 7.2. Additional Efficacy Considerations
L413: ## 7.2.1. Considerations on Benefit in the Postmarket Setting
L414: The population enrolled in Studies AACG and AACI did not include patients at either end of the Alzheimer's disease continuum (Stage 1-2 or Stage 5-6 as defined by the 2024 FDA Draft Guidance for Early Alzheimer's Disease) and there is some uncertainty with respect to the generalizability of benefit across the entire spectrum of Alzheimer's disease. However, there is a general expectation, and the scientific evidence to date supports, that initiating treatment with donanemab earlier in the disease may provide the best opportunity to delay or halt the pathophysiological processes that lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease. The ongoing study (AACM) of donanemab in individuals at risk for cognitive and function decline of Alzheimer's disease should address the potential benefit in this population. Intervention with donanemab later in the disease may be expected to provide less benefit, as downstream pathological processes may dominate.
L415: Individuals with Down syndrome represent another important population at risk for Alzheimer's disease who might also benefit from treatment with donanemab. Alzheimer's disease in individuals with Down syndrome is likely driven by an overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein located on chromosome 21, thus the pathology in this population is similar to that found in dominantly inherited Alzheimer's disease and sporadic Alzheimer's disease. One challenge is assessing changes in cognition and function in a population with intellectual disability. Also, individuals with Down syndrome have a higher incidence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Therefore, additional safety data would be needed to inform risk-benefit considerations in this population.
L416: An important consideration for the use of donanemab is that dosing was stopped once amyloid levels were reduced below a certain quantitative threshold on PET imaging. Although subjects continued to show benefit compared to placebo after dosing was stopped, the follow up period is relatively short and there is no information on whether subjects would have shown greater benefit if they had continued dosing. It was shown that amyloid plaques can re-accumulate at low rates following the cessation of therapy. There remains uncertainty regarding the optimal treatment regimen for donanemab once amyloid levels have been reduced to a level that corresponds with a "negative" visual read on PET. Labeling should reflect the uncertainties regarding the optimal duration of treatment. This residual uncertainty also warrants a postmarketing study of the effectiveness of donanemab in subjects who have completed treatment based on amyloid plaque levels and the potential need for re-initiation of treatment or a maintenance regimen to maintain the reduction of amyloid plaque.
L417: ## 7.3. Integrated Assessment of Effectiveness
L418: The evidence submitted in support of effectiveness is derived from randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials of donanemab in patients at the early stages of symptomatic Alzheimer's disease.
L419: Study AACI is an adequate and well-controlled, large multicenter trial with positive and statistically very persuasive results on the primary endpoint, iADRS, and on all multiplicity-controlled secondary clinical endpoints (CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog 13 and ADCS-iADL). These secondary endpoints partly capture distinct information regarding cognitive decline and impact on daily function and support the overall clinical meaningfulness of the results. The treatment effect was apparent by the 3-month visit and the absolute treatment difference tended to increase with time. The robustness of the observed treatment effect was demonstrated by sensitivity analyses, including one assessing the potential for functional unblinding. The treatment effect in Study AACI is supported by the consistently favorable results for the primary and secondary endpoints across subgroups of interest defined by demographic and baseline disease characteristics. Biomarkers reflecting brain amyloid plaque load and astrocytic activation support the observations on the clinical endpoints.
L420: It is useful to interpret treatment difference as a percent reduction rather than the absolute point difference which depends on the length of the study and the disease stage. The results of Study AACI demonstrate a reduced decline of approximately 20% to 30% on clinical endpoints in the combined population. For CDR-SB, this corresponds to a preservation of CDR-SB by approximately 5.4 months relative to placebo over the 18 months of the study. This preservation of cognitive function is clearly clinically meaningful. Further context is provided by the analysis demonstrating a 37% reduction in the risk of progression on the global CDR score and the higher responder rate (CDR-SB change from baseline \le 0) for subjects treated with donanemab.
L421: Study AACG is a smaller adequate and well-controlled study which achieved statistical significance on the primary endpoint, iADRS. Despite not reaching statistical significance according to the prespecified hierarchy, the estimates of the treatment effect at Week 76 across secondary endpoints are consistent with the reduction of clinical decline observed in Study AACI. The effect of donanemab on brain amyloid plaque demonstrated in Study AACG was robust and persuasive and supported the design of Study AACI. The results of Study AACG provide independent substantiation for the benefits observed in Study AACI.
L422: ## 8. Review of Safety
L423: Please see the separate safety review by Dr. Branagan.
L424: ## 9. Advisory Committee Meeting and Other External Consultations
L425: An advisory committee meeting was held on June 10, 2024, to discuss whether the data from Study AACI support a favorable benefit-risk assessment for the use of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
L426: The committee discussed whether the available data provided evidence of effectiveness of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and commented on the support for effectiveness across tau PET subgroups, including the no/very low tau population that was excluded from the placebo-controlled trials. The committee voted unanimously, 11-0, that the data show that donanemab is effective for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. Most committee members thought biomarker effects in patients enrolled in the Study AACI safety addendum supported efficacy in patients with no or very low tau. There was also general consensus that requiring tau PET would be impractical to implement and would impede access to treatment.
L427: The committee also discussed the dosing regimen used in the clinical trials and if there were scientific and/or clinical considerations that may factor into a decision to stop or continue dosing with donanemab. The committee members agreed that the dosing regimen guided by reduction of amyloid plaque on PET imaging was an innovative component of the clinical trial design that could provide potential benefits for compliance and reduced burden on patients and the health care system. However, members were in agreement that more long-term data is needed to address questions on duration of amyloid clearance, how frequently patients would need to be monitored after stopping donanemab, when treatment should be re-initiated, and potential adverse effects of stopping and restarting therapy.
L428: The committee also discussed the overall risk-benefit of donanemab and voted unanimously, 11-0, that the benefits of donanemab outweigh its risks for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

L501: ## 3.2. Summary of Presubmission/Submission Regulatory Activity
L502: The Applicant submitted BLA 761248 on May 18, 2022, and on January 18, 2022, received a complete response letter from the Division, based on an insufficient safety database to characterize the long-term safety of donanemab. The Division had expected the BLA submission to have at least 100 subjects exposed to drug for \ge 12 months, consistent with ICH E1 guidelines, to adequately characterize the safety of donanemab. The BLA submission contained data for 49 subjects who were exposed to donanemab at the highest proposed dosage regimen (700 mg for 3 doses followed by 1400 mg thereafter) for 12 months. Additionally, it was noted that the majority of the 6-month safety exposures were from uncontrolled data from open-label studies.
L503: The contents of this resubmission contain the unblinded controlled data from the Phase 3 Study AACI.

The reader is referred to the Issues Regarding Data Integrity and Submission Quality section of this review for further details.
L543: The placebo-controlled period of Study AACI was the primary source for evidence of efficacy and results from this period of the study were analyzed separately from other studies. Results from Study AACG and the placebo-controlled period of Study AACI were pooled to create a placebo-controlled pool for safety analyses. AACI Study Addendum and the two open-label studies, AACH Part B and AACN-Dona Cohort, were pooled with donanemab-treated subjects from Studies AACG and AACI (placebo-controlled and long-term extension periods) to create an all-donanemab-treated pool, which allows for analysis of adverse events occurring with exposure to donanemab for up to 12 months.
L544: Study AACG was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of donanemab in patients with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease and mild Alzheimer's dementia. The study was comprised of a 9-week screening period, an up to 72-week treatment
L545: period with final evaluations occurring 4 weeks later at Week 76, and a 48-week follow-up period. Subjects were randomized to either donanemab 700 mg intravenously for the first three doses, then 1400 mg every four weeks for up to 72 weeks or to placebo intravenously every four weeks for up to 72 weeks.1
L546: In Study AACG, donanemab doses could be modified based on amyloid plaque reduction measured by florbetapir PET imaging. Depending on the degree of amyloid plaque reduction noted at Week 24 or Week 52, donanemab doses could be reduced from 1400 mg to 700 mg or the subject could be switched to placebo.
L547: The main study of Study AACI enrolled patients with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease and mild Alzheimer's dementia and was comprised of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled period and a double-blind long-term extension period. The study included an up to 7-week screening period, an up to 76-week double-blind period (treatment up to 72 weeks) and a 78-week extension period (treatment up to 72 weeks), and a 44-week follow-up period. In the placebo-controlled period, subjects were randomized to either donanemab 700 mg intravenously for the first three doses, then 1400 mg every four weeks for up to 72 weeks or to placebo intravenously every four weeks for up to 72 weeks. Subjects could be switched from donanemab to placebo if they met dose reduction criteria based on amyloid plaque reduction measured by florbetapir F18 PET scans. In the long-term extension period, subjects randomized to donanemab in the placebo-controlled period who had not met dose reduction criteria by Week 76 were assigned to receive donanemab. Subjects randomized to donanemab in the placebo-controlled period who had met dose reduction criteria by Week 76 were assigned placebo. Subjects randomized to placebo in the placebo-controlled period were assigned to receive donanemab in the same dose titration as subjects in the placebo-controlled period.
L548: Study AACG differed from the other studies in that the donanemab dose could be reduced to 700 mg based on meeting amyloid plaque reduction criteria, rather than being discontinued or changed to placebo.

L554: ## Analysis of Adverse Events
L555: Mortality analyses were based on an on-study approach and included all deaths reported by the end of the study period (76 weeks for the placebo-controlled period of Study AACCI), regardless of whether the patient discontinued from the study period.
L556: For analyses not related to mortality, adverse events were included if they were considered treatment-emergent and occurred while the subject was on study drug or within 57 days of the last dose of the study drug (where 57 days is approximately 5-times the half-life of donanemab).
L557: Adverse events in this review were evaluated by preferred term and by groupings of closely related preferred terms called EMQ and FMQ groupings. The reader is referred to the Appendix for a list of EMQ and FMQ groupings in this review and the preferred terms that make up the groupings.
L558: ## Adverse Events of Special Interest
L559: Amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), hypersensitivity reactions, and infusion related reactions are topics of special interest for the safety review of donanemab based on the safety profile of aducanumab and lecanemab, amyloid-directed monoclonal antibody drugs approved for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.3,4
L560: Immunogenicity is also a topic of special interest for this review, based on the observation of infusion related reactions occurring in Phase 1 studies with donanemab.

L565: ## 8.2.1. Overall Exposure
L566: Overall, the Applicant met ICH guidelines of at least 300 subjects exposed to the highest clinically relevant doses that is the proposed dose for labeling (700 mg every 4 weeks for 3 doses followed by 1400 mg every 4 weeks) for six months and 100 subjects for one year. At the time of the 90-Day Safety, 1912 subjects in the all-donanemab pool were exposed to donanemab for 6 months and 1057 subjects for 12 months. The safety database includes 2899 subjects exposed to at least one dose of donanemab at any dose or route of administration, of whom 2891 received at least 1 dose intravenously. There were 2885 subjects with Alzheimer's disease exposed to donanemab intravenously.
L567: The dosing proposed in labeling allows for continued dosing of donanemab every 4 weeks, with decisions for continued dosing based on judgement that may be informed by amyloid imaging. This is different from dosing in the primary clinical studies for safety, AACG and AACI, in which some subjects completed a course of treatment in less than 12 months because of the dosing paradigm that either stopped or reduced dosing with donanemab once a threshold of reduction in amyloid on PET imaging was reached. Some subjects were treated longer than 12 months if they did not reach the threshold for amyloid reduction at an earlier timepoint.

L643: ## 8.3.2. Categorization of Adverse Events
L644: This reviewer notes that the method of recording AEs of ARIA-H in the adverse event datasets likely underrepresent the incidence of ARIA-H experienced by subjects in Studies AACG, AACH,
L645: and AACI, and that data from MRIs likely provides a better approximation of the incidence of ARIA-H. This reviewer considered the definitions for TEAEs and SAEs to be acceptable. Translation of verbatim terms for adverse events to MedDRA preferred terms was adequate, except as noted below for four subjects including one subject with an adverse event of intracerebral hemorrhage.
L646: As noted in this reviewer's Safety Review dated January 17, 2023, ARIA events were recorded as adverse events and as MRI findings in AACG and AACI. ARIA-E findings were required to be reported as adverse events by investigators, but this was not specified for ARIA-H events. This reviewer considered the dataset containing MRI findings to be the more comprehensive dataset for ARIA findings and as a result, analyses related to ARIA and intracerebral hemorrhage use the MRI dataset unless otherwise specified.
L647: Analyses of adverse events for this review used the integrated database.
L648: In the ISS, the Applicant's analyses of adverse events of the pooled placebo-controlled studies and the all-donanemab pool used the integrated database, whereas the Applicant's analyses of adverse events occurring in Study AACI used the AACI database. Differences in the Applicant's definition of baseline in the integrated database compared to Study AACI database resulted in differences in the numbers of adverse events considered treatment-emergent. In Study AACI adverse events were considered baseline if they occurred *prior to* the informed consent date in contrast to the IDB where adverse events were considered baseline if they occurred *up to* the informed consent date.14
L649: Adverse events in the integrated database were coded to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 25.1.
L650: The protocol for Study AACI specified that all adverse events occurring after signing of the informed consent form were to be recorded in the case report form. Adverse events were collected at every visit, which occurred every four weeks during the placebo-controlled and long-term extension periods, and then quarterly during the follow-up period (starting 12 weeks after the last dose of investigational product). The protocol specified that for adverse events that were serious or were AEs of special interest, the subject should be followed until the event resolves, stabilizes, or is reasonably explained or the subject was lost to follow-up. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined as untoward medical occurrence that emerged during a defined treatment period, having been absent pretreatment (prior to the informed consent date), or worsens relative to the pretreatment state, and does not necessarily have a causal relationship with the treatment. A serious adverse event (SAE) was defined as any AE that result in death, initial or prolonged inpatient hospitalization, was life-threatening,
L651: 14 Noted in the Applicant's response dated July 24, 2023, to an information request dated July 21, 2023.
L652: persistent disability/incapacity, congenital anomaly/birth defect, or an important medical event that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalization but may jeopardize the subject or may require intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed above. Adverse events were coded to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 25.1.

L662: ## 8.4.1. Deaths
L663: In the placebo-controlled period of AACI, using an on study approach for evaluation, mortality at 76 weeks occurred in 2.2% (17/853) of subjects randomized to donanemab and in 1.2% (10/874) of subjects randomized to placebo, risk difference (95% CI) 1.0% (-0.3%, 2.3%), hazard ratio (95% CI) 1.80 (0.83, 3.94).16 Taking into consideration three amyloid related imaging abnormalities-related deaths, which occurred in donanemab-treated patients, the non-ARIA related mortality at 76 weeks occurred in 1.8% (14/853) of subjects randomized to donanemab and in 1.2% (10/874) of subjects randomized to placebo, risk difference (95% CI) 0.6% (-0.6%, 1.8%), hazard ratio (95% CI) 1.49 (0.66, 3.35).17 Data from participants who continued into the LTE or were newly started on donanemab from placebo in the Safety Addendum were included in the All-Donanemab pool. In the all-donanemab pool, the deaths occurred in 1.3% (37/2802).18

L669: In the placebo-controlled period of Study AACI, approximately 26% of donanemab-treated patients withdrew from the study compared to 20% on placebo. After withdrawing from the study, vital status at Week 76 was not captured for these patients by the Applicant.
L670: *Reviewer comment: The lack of vital status information collected during the conduct of Study AACI added uncertainty to the mortality analysis, for which there was an imbalance in deaths observed with donanemab relative to placebo.*
L671: With high rates of missing vital status data at Week 76 and its potential impact on the assessment of mortality, the Division requested that the Applicant retrieve additional mortality information among patients who discontinued Study AACI prior to Week 76 and for whom the vital status was not available at the time of the 90-Day safety update. Using a third-party vendor, the applicant retrieved vital status through publicly available records and databases, social media, and traditional media. Information on cause of death is still not available. Among 352 participants (198 for donanemab and 154 for placebo) whose vital status was unknown, the vital status of 52% (184 participants) was retrieved: 118 for donanemab and 66 for placebo, respectively. Among the participants with retrieved vital status information, two participants randomized to donanemab died within 76 weeks and six participants randomized to placebo died within 76 weeks.
L672: Incorporating these retrieved deaths into the deaths observed during the trial resulted in 19 deaths on donanemab and 16 deaths on placebo.
L673: Limitations of these data include that the additional death information was obtained through a different approach from the approach planned in Study AACI, and included publicly available information in records, databases, social media, and traditional media. Additionally, approximately 10% of patients still had missing vital status information and the retrieved vital status information lacked information on the cause of death.

L678: As deaths are not uncommon in the population of older adults typically enrolled in AD trials, it is useful to consider the imbalance of deaths observed in AACI with mortality findings from other recent placebo-controlled clinical trials of amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies, which are shown in the table below. The studies were comparable in terms of age of the subjects and ApoE ε4 genotype. Clinical trials with donanemab compared to other monoclonal antibodies included a population with more advanced disease (higher proportion of subjects with mild AD compared to mild cognitive impairment, with 82% of subjects in the placebo-controlled pool for donanemab having mild AD at baseline compared to 38% in pooled trials for lecanemab and 45% in pooled trials for gantenerumab)).20,21 Overall, there is not a signal for mortality in other drugs in the class of amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies.
L679: When comparing AACI to individual studies, it is important to consider the time period when the studies were conducted as the COVID pandemic has been shown to impact mortality rates in clinical trials broadly. For donanemab, AACG took place from 2017-2020 and AACI took place from 2020-2023. Of the trials listed, the gantenerumab trials were conducted in a time period

Overall, the comparison to other AD trials shows that mortality rates can vary across studies, and that the mortality rates in AACI in the placebo arm are within the background rate of deaths reported in placebo arms across multiple studies.

L690: The mortality rate observed in donanemab-treated subjects in the placebo-controlled period of AACI or the all-donanemab pool did not exceed the mortality rate observed in a U.S. population of community-dwelling people with Alzheimer's disease; however, the clinical trial population was likely healthier than the community-dwelling population with AD based on population inclusion and exclusion criteria. Based on the 90-Day Safety Update database cutoff date of June 7, 2023, incidence of death by person-years of exposure to donanemab in the placebo-controlled period of AACI is 15.0/1,000 person-years (17/1137.0 person-years) and in the all-
L691: donanemab pool is 15.9/1,000 person-years (37/2322 person-years).22 In a 15-year prospective cohort study of subjects age &gt; 65 years or older, the mortality rate in subjects with Alzheimer's disease (unadjusted for age or sex) was observed to be 133.8/1,000 person-years23, and was higher than that observed in the placebo-controlled period of AACI or the all-donanemab pool. The populations in the placebo-controlled period of AACI and the all-donanemab pool were likely healthier than the cohort population studied given that patients were excluded if they had a more advanced stage of AD, serious or unstable illnesses, other significant neurological disease affecting the central nervous system other than Alzheimer's disease, or a life expectancy of &lt; 24 months, among other criteria.
L692: ARIA-related deaths occurred in 0.4% (3/853) of donanemab-treated subjects in AACI compared to none in placebo. In one of these subjects, intracerebral hemorrhage occurred with ARIA-E and ARIA-H in the setting of findings that can be seen with cerebral amyloid angiopathy (see table below). In the all-donanemab pool, there was an additional death associated with ARIA and an additional death associated with intracerebral hemorrhage that occurred in a subject with ARIA-E, with symptoms mimicking stroke who was treated with thrombolytic therapy. There was no other unusual cluster of deaths in the database.

L760: *Reviewer comment: Thrombolytic use is a risk factor for intracerebral hemorrhage in this case. The relationship of intracerebral hemorrhage to donanemab in this setting of treatment with tenecteplase is uncertain.*

L958: ## 8.5.2. ARIA and Intracerebral Hemorrhage
L959: Monoclonal antibodies directed against aggregated forms of beta amyloid, can cause ARIA, characterized as ARIA with edema (ARIA-E), observed on MRI as brain edema or sulcal effusions, and ARIA with hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H), which includes microhemorrhage and superficial siderosis. ARIA-H can occur spontaneously in people with Alzheimer's disease. ARIA-H of any cause and ARIA-E may occur in isolation or together; ARIA-H associated with monoclonal antibodies directed against aggregated forms of beta amyloid generally occurs in association with an occurrence of ARIA-E. The following section focuses on findings of ARIA and intracerebral hemorrhage observed in donanemab clinical trials.
L960: The reader is referred to the Appendix for definitions and management of ARIA.
L961: ## Methods
L962: ARIA events were recorded as adverse events and as MRI findings AACG and AACI. ARIA-E findings were required to be reported as adverse events by investigators, but this was not specified for ARIA-H events. Symptoms associated with ARIA-E, seriousness of ARIA events, and ARIA events reported to lead to study withdrawal and treatment discontinuation were recorded in the adverse event dataset.40 Given that the different datasets recorded different information, analyses in this section of the review will specify whether the analysis was based on the adverse event dataset or the MRI dataset.
L963: *Reviewer comment: In estimating the incidence of ARIA-H, this reviewer considered the dataset containing MRI findings to be the more comprehensive dataset for ARIA findings, in agreement with the applicant's approach. This reviewer considered the adverse event dataset to be the*
L964: 40 Input for the MRI dataset was based on information collected from MRI worksheets. A sample MRI Brain Worksheet from Study AACI was included in the Applicant's response dated October 3, 2023, to an information request dated October 2, 2023.

L1053: ## ARIA and Intracerebral Hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm by ApoE \epsilon4 Genotype Status
L1054: ApoE \epsilon4 homozygotes have been previously shown to have an increased incidence of symptomatic and overall ARIA compared to heterozygotes and noncarriers in subjects taking monoclonal antibodies directed against aggregated forms of beta amyloid.
L1055: In the placebo-controlled period of AACI and the placebo-controlled pool, donanemab-treated homozygote ApoE \epsilon4 carriers had an increased incidence of ARIA, ARIA-E, and ARIA-H Microhemorrhage, and ARIA-H superficial siderosis compared to heterozygotes and noncarriers. Homozygous carriers in the all-donanemab pool had similar incidences of ARIA, ARIA-E, ARIA-H, ARIA-H Microhemorrhage, and ARIA-H Superficial siderosis (difference no greater than 6%) compared to the placebo-controlled period of AACI.
L1056: Limited numbers of events of intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm (n=4, within 57 days of a dose) in the placebo-controlled period of AACI preclude a conclusion being drawn regarding the impact of donanemab in ApoE \epsilon4 carriers on incidence of intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm. Additionally, two of the four donanemab-treated subjects with intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm had concomitant medication use with an antithrombotic, which further limits a conclusion being drawn of the effect of ApoE \epsilon4 status on incidence of intracerebral hemorrhage. ApoE \epsilon4 alleles have been associated with an increased risk of intracerebral hemorrhage.45

The reader is referred to the Appendix for analyses of the incidence of ARIA and intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm in the placebo-controlled pool.

L1076: ## ApoE \epsilon4 Genotype Status and Timing of ARIA (MRI dataset)
L1077: Homozygous ApoE \epsilon4 carriers had similar incidences of developing ARIA-E within the first three and first six doses compared to all donanemab-treated subjects in the placebo-controlled pool (differences no greater than 2%). The reader is referred to the Appendix for analyses related to number of doses received to first ARIA-E in ApoE \epsilon4 carriers.
L1078: Among donanemab-treated subjects homozygous for ApoE \epsilon4, the majority of first ARIA-E events had occurred by 400 days from first treatment in the placebo-controlled period of AACI (approximately 15 doses). The following plot shows the probability of first ARIA-E event by ApoE \epsilon4 status among donanemab-treated subjects in the placebo-controlled period of AACI.

L1082: ## Other Risk Factors for ARIA
L1083: In analyses of the placebo-controlled pool submitted by the Applicant, donanemab-treated subjects with microhemorrhage or superficial siderosis on baseline MRI had a higher incidence of ARIA compared to subjects without those findings on baseline MRI (53.1% [78/147] versus 33.3% [279/837], respectively).46
L1084: 46 Noted on page 1073 of the Applicant's response dated October 10, 2023, to an information request dated October 2, 2023.
L1085: In analyses of the placebo-controlled pool submitted by the Applicant, donanemab-treated subjects with white matter disease present on baseline MRI had higher incidence of ARIA in compared to subjects without those findings (37.4% [333/890] versus 25.5% [24/94], respectively).47
L1086: Using the data from the all-donanemab pool, the applicant identified the presence of 2-4 microhemorrhages at baseline and presence of 1 area of superficial siderosis at baseline as risk factors for ARIA-E and for ARIA-H, in addition to the number of ApoE \epsilon4 alleles.48 Of note, there are limitations of these analyses in that the study excluded patients with severe white matter lesions, more than 4 microhemorrhages, and more than 1 area of superficial siderosis. Nevertheless, the risk factors were able to be identified, even with more severe pathology excluded.

L1091: In studies AACH, AACG, and AACI, antithrombotic use was allowed. For the following analyses, subjects were considered to have used antithrombotics if they reported use within 30 days prior to an event of ARIA-H or intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm.

The incidence of intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm in donanemab-treated subjects on antithrombotics was slightly greater than in those not on antithrombotics (0.6% versus 0.4%, respectively). L1110: ## Thrombolytic Use and Intracerebral Hemorrhage
L1111: One donanemab-treated subject developed intracerebral hemorrhage with fatal outcome in the setting of thrombolytic use (tenecteplase) for symptoms mimicking stroke in the setting of ARIA-E (intracerebral hemorrhage, I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)). The contribution of donanemab to the event in this case is unknown. It is important for physicians to recognize that a patient has been exposed to donanemab when presenting with stroke-like symptoms. The case is discussed further in the Deaths section of this review.
L1112: Concomitant administration of tPA was reported for 3 additional subjects, none of whom had intracerebral hemorrhage (donanemab: I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) and placebo: I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) and I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)). The donanemab-treated subject had fatal outcome from complications of Covid-19, and also experienced cerebral infarction in the setting of atrial fibrillation. The case is discussed further in the Deaths section of this review.
L1113: ## 8.5.3. Seizure
L1114: The incidence of seizures was greater in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in the setting of ARIA as well as independent of ARIA in the placebo-controlled period of AACI and the placebo-controlled pool. No events of status epilepticus were observed.
L1115: ## Method
L1116: For the following analyses, this reviewer analyzed seizures recorded in the adverse event dataset and the clinical event analysis dataset, which recorded any symptoms associated with ARIA. For events of intracerebral hemorrhage, this reviewer analyzed events recorded in both
L1117: the adverse event dataset and the MRI dataset. For events of ARIA, this reviewer analyzed ARIA events recorded in the adverse event dataset, which this reviewer considered to be the most comprehensive source for recording symptoms associated with ARIA.
L1118: A higher incidence of seizure was observed in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI (1.2% versus 0.3%, respectively). Among donanemab-treated subjects with seizure, seizure as a symptom of ARIA-E accounted for 50% of the cases (5/10). An imbalance in serious cases of seizure was observed in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo (0.4% versus 0.1%, respectively). No cases of seizure were reported in the setting of intracerebral hemorrhage in the placebo-controlled period of AACI. A higher incidence of seizure occurring independently of either ARIA or intracerebral hemorrhage was observed among donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI (0.6% versus 0.3%, respectively). Similar findings were observed for the placebo-controlled pool. A similar incidence of seizure was observed in the all-donanemab pool compared to the placebo-controlled period of AACI (difference no greater than 0.5%). No events of status epilepticus were reported.

L1124: ## Narratives
L1125: This reviewer identified nine SAEs related to the topic seizure, occurring in 8 subjects in the all-donanemab pool using the within treatment period plus 57 days analysis method.
L1126: In one case, this reviewer did not establish a role for donanemab in the event of seizure as the event occurred more than 200 days after the last dose of study drug (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)).
L1127: In a review of narratives, this reviewer noted one additional subject with seizure that occurred in the setting of ARIA-E with fatal outcome (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)).50 In this case, the cause of death was reported as secondary to symptomatic ARIA-E, aggravated by seizures.
L1128: In one case, seizure occurred in the setting of ARIA-E and 5 new microhemorrhages in a subject with a total of 23 microhemorrhages and with superficial siderosis and resulted in discontinuation of donanemab (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)).
L1129: In one case, the seizure occurred in a subject who had developed diabetic ketoacidosis (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)).
L1130: In two cases, this reviewer did not rule out a role for donanemab given the imbalance in seizure noted in the placebo-controlled pool. In these two cases, the subjects continued to receive donanemab without experiencing further seizures (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) and I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)).
L1131: In the remaining cases of seizure, although a role for donanemab could not be ruled out given the imbalance noted in the placebo-controlled pool, this reviewer identified other potential contributory factors, including recent event of hemorrhagic stroke (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)), metabolic encephalopathy and Covid-19 infection (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)), and falls/subarachnoid bleed/subdural hygromas/moderate ARIA-H (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)). The reader is referred to the Appendix for a narrative for this case.
L1132: ## 8.5.4. Hypersensitivity and Infusion Related Reactions
L1133: Infusion related reactions were among the most frequently reported TEAEs in the placebo-controlled period of AACI, occurring in 8.7% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to 0.5% on placebo. Symptoms associated with infusion-related reactions included: chills, erythema, nausea/vomiting, dyspnea, sweating, elevated blood pressure, headache, chest pain, and low blood pressure. Hypersensitivity reactions other than infusion related reactions occurred in 2.9% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to 0.7% on placebo and included anaphylaxis and angioedema. Most infusion-related reactions and other hypersensitivity reactions were
L1134: 50 Event not recorded in the adverse event or symptomatic ARIA-E dataset.
L1135: mild or moderate in severity in the placebo-controlled period of AACI, the placebo-controlled pool, and the all-donanemab pool. Serious cases of infusion related reactions and other hypersensitivity events included cases with increases and decreases in blood pressure and increases in heart rate at the time of infusion or within minutes following the end of the infusion. In one case, increases in blood pressure in the setting of infusion reactions was associated with myocardial infarction.
L1136: ## Method
L1137: The Applicant's method for analysis of adverse events related to the topic of hypersensitivity and infusion related reactions included evaluations of TEAEs belonging to the SMOs of Anaphylactic Reaction (Narrow), Hypersensitivity (Narrow), and Angioedema (Narrow).
L1138: *Reviewer comment: Overall, this reviewer found the Applicant's approach to be acceptable.*

L1155: ## Interventions for Infusion Related Reactions
L1156: The following information was provided by the Applicant in the 90-Day Safety Update Resubmission Safety Update Report dated September 9, 2023 (Section 4.5.1.2.4 Infusion-Related Reactions and Interventions, page 84).
L1157: The Applicant noted that interventions for infusion related reactions included administration of medications prior to infusion and slowing of the infusion on or after the infusion related reaction.
L1158: Pretreatment medications for infusion related reactions included antihistamines, acetaminophen, and corticosteroids.
L1159: The Applicant compared the incidence of infusion related reactions among subjects who received medications pretreatment upon rechallenge to subjects who did not receive pretreatment medication upon rechallenge in the all-donanemab pool.

In one case, the subject had a history of inflammatory bowel disease and the symptom of diarrhea preceded the initial donanemab dose as a risk factor for microscopic colitis (microscopic colitis, I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b)(6)).68 This subject also experienced the SAE of acute pancreatitis 8 days later, which is discussed in the Serious Adverse Events section of this review. In the second case with TEAE of microscopic colitis, a role for donanemab could not be established given concomitant ibuprofen use, which has been associated with colitis (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b)(6)).69 The reader is referred to the Appendix for further details of this case. In one of the cases with TEAE of enterocolitis, the subject had the concurrent AE of norovirus test positive, which was the likely cause for the enterocolitis (enterocolitis, I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b)(6)). The second case with TEAE of enterocolitis was attributed to a viral etiology (viral enterocolitis, I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b)(6)).

L1333: ## 8.9. Safety in the Postmarket Setting
L1334: ## 8.9.1. Safety Concerns Identified Through Postmarket Experience
L1335: Not applicable. Donanemab is a new molecular entity. It is not approved in other regions of the
L1336: world.
L1337: ## 8.9.2. Expectations on Safety in the Postmarket Setting
L1338: In clinical trials, donanemab was administered until amyloid reduction criteria were met. In the proposed label, no endpoints for ending dosing with donanemab are included. The risk of donanemab use in patients who meet amyloid reduction criteria used in clinical trials has not been assessed.
L1339: The population studied was relatively healthy, had mild cognitive impairment or mild AD. A low number of subjects with age &lt; 65 years or age 85 years or older were enrolled. The risk of using donanemab in a population &lt; 65 years of age or ≥85 years of age, a population with advanced comorbidities, or a population with more advanced stages of AD could be higher.
L1340: The population studies was predominantly White and not Hispanic or Latino. Due to the low number of subjects who were not of the White race or of Hispanic or Latino ethnicity, the safety of donanemab in these populations is unknown.
L1341: Patients with baseline MRIs that demonstrated presence of ARIA-E, &gt; 4 cerebral microhemorrhages, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, any macrohemorrhage or severe white matter disease were not studied. The safety profile of donanemab, including risk for ARIA and intracerebral hemorrhage, in these populations is unknown.
L1342: There are limited safety data related to continuing treatment with donanemab in patients who have experienced multiple episodes of ARIA-E. There is limited experience in continued dosing through symptomatic, radiographically mild ARIA-E that is allowed for in the approved label and that is the current class approach to dosing.73
L1343: There are limited safety data in patients who received thrombolytics while on treatment with donanemab.
L1344: Subjects who experienced events of intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm while on treatment with donanemab did not receive additional doses of donanemab after the events of intracerebral hemorrhage. The safety of continued treatment with donanemab in patients who have experienced intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm while on donanemab therapy is unknown.
L1345: Assessments for human carcinogenicity were limited by the period of observation for subjects in the all-donanemab pool (median duration of ~500 days). The carcinogenic risk profile for donanemab with durations of treatment longer than what was studied is unknown.
L1346: 73 January 12, 2024, Response to information request.
L1347: The evaluation of safety in the placebo-controlled period of AACI and the placebo-controlled pool was limited by the percentage of subjects who withdrew from the study (approximately 27% of subjects in the donanemab arm and 20% on placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI and 27% and 21%, respectively, for the placebo-controlled pool). The analyses of safety may underestimate the incidence of adverse reactions with donanemab. However, of the subjects lost to follow-up, AEs at the last contact were not serious.

L1350: ## 8.10. Integrated Assessment of Safety
L1351: Safety findings from BLA 761248 are summarized below.
L1352: Relevant characteristics of the safety population. Patients with moderate or severe dementia were not included in AACG and AACI. Treatment was discontinued in clinical studies once subjects met criteria for amyloid plaque reduction. In the placebo-controlled period of AACI and the placebo-controlled pool, a low number of subjects were enrolled with the following demographic characteristics: age less than 65 years, age 85 years or older, non-White race, and Hispanic or Latino ethnicity. Conclusions regarding the impact of these demographic characteristics on the frequency of adverse events cannot be drawn.
L1353: Adequacy of the safety database. The safety database met ICH E1A guidelines for exposure of at least 300 subjects at 6 months and 100 subjects at 12 months at the proposed dose.
L1354: Deaths. In the placebo-controlled period of AACI, using the on study approach to evaluation, mortality at 76 weeks occurred in 2.2% (17/853) of subjects randomized to donanemab and in 1.2% (10/874) of subjects randomized to placebo, hazard ratio (95% CI) 1.79 (0.82, 3.93). Two deaths in the donanemab arm were attributed to ARIA. Intracerebral hemorrhage occurred in 1 subject with ARIA-H in the setting of findings that can be seen with cerebral amyloid angiopathy. In the all-donanemab pool, the incidence of deaths was 1.3%, with an additional death associated with ARIA and an additional death associated with intracerebral hemorrhage that occurred in a subject with ARIA-E, with symptoms mimicking stroke who was treated with thrombolytic therapy. There was no other unusual cluster of deaths in the database.
L1355: SAEs. A higher incidence of subjects reported SAEs in the donanemab arm compared to placebo in the placebo-controlled pool (16% versus 14%, respectively). ARIA-E and pneumonia were the SAEs reported with higher incidence in the donanemab arm compared to placebo and greatest difference in the placebo-controlled pool. ARIA-E was reported in 1.5% of subjects in the donanemab arm compared to none on placebo. Pneumonia was reported in 1% of subjects in the donanemab arm compared to 0.3% on placebo. In the all-donanemab pool, ARIA-E was the preferred term reported with highest incidence, occurring in 1.1% of subjects.
L1356: AEs Leading to Drug or Study Discontinuations. Approximately 26% of subjects in the donanemab arm and 20% on placebo withdrew from the study in the placebo-controlled period
L1357: of AACI. A higher incidence of donanemab-treated subjects reported adverse events leading to study withdrawal compared to placebo, occurring in 8% of subjects on donanemab versus 3% on placebo. Infusion related reaction, ARIA-E, and ARIA-H microhemorrhage were reported to lead to study withdrawal with highest incidence and greatest difference in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in AACI. Adverse events lead to treatment discontinuation in 30% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to 20% on placebo in Study AACI. Infusion related reaction and ARIA-E were adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation with highest incidence in the donanemab arm and greatest difference from placebo in Study AACI.
L1358: Significant AEs. Evaluation of severe AEs did not identify a new safety signal.
L1359: Most Common AEs. ARIA-E, ARIA-H Microhemorrhage, ARIA-H Superficial Siderosis, infusion related reaction, and headache were TEAEs reported with highest incidence in the donanemab arm and greatest difference from placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI, occurring with incidence of at least 5% in the donanemab arm and at least 2% greater than placebo: ARIA-E (24% and 2% on donanemab and placebo, respectively), ARIA-H Microhemorrhage (25% and 11% on donanemab and placebo, respectively), ARIA-H Superficial Siderosis (15% and 3% on donanemab and placebo, respectively), infusion related reaction (9% and 0.5% on donanemab and placebo, respectively), and headache (13% and 10% on donanemab and placebo, respectively). AEs occurring in less than 5% of donanemab-treated subjects and at least 2% more than placebo in Study AACI included hypersensitivity reactions, intestinal obstruction, and intestinal perforation.
L1360: Vital sign, laboratory, and ECG evaluations in the placebo-controlled pool showed a slightly higher incidence of alkaline phosphatase \ge 2 times the upper limit of normal in the donanemab arm compared to placebo (0.6% versus 0.2%).
L1361: Pre-specified AE of interest:
L1362: Hepatic Safety – An imbalance in alkaline phosphatase \ge 2 times the upper limit of normal was observed in the placebo-controlled pool; however, the absolute difference in incidence between the donanemab and placebo arm was small (0.6% versus 0.2%, respectively). A review of narratives of subjects with hepatic enzyme elevation did not identify a safety signal for hepatotoxicity.
L1363: Immunogenicity - In the all-donanemab pool, 88% of subjects who were evaluable for treatment emergent anti-drug antibody (ADA) responses had a positive postbaseline treatment emergent ADA status. All of these subjects also had neutralizing antibody present.
L1364: ARIA – ARIA has been observed in other amyloid-directed monoclonal antibody therapies for the treatment of AD. In the placebo-controlled period of AACI, three cases of ARIA had fatal outcome. One additional fatal case of ARIA was observed in the all-donanemab pool. Serious ARIA-E cases were reported in 1.5% of subjects in the placebo-controlled period of AACI.
L1365: Symptomatic ARIA-E was reported in 6% of subjects in the placebo-controlled period of AACI. Intracerebral hemorrhage &gt; 1 cm was reported in eight subjects (0.3%) in the all-donanemab pool.
L1366: Seizure – A higher incidence of seizure independent of ARIA was observed in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI (0.6% versus
L1367: 0.3%, respectively). Seizure as a symptom of ARIA was reported in 0.6% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to none on placebo.
L1368: Hypersensitivity and infusion-related reactions – Infusion related reaction was reported in 8.7% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to 0.5% on placebo in Study AACI. Increases and decreases in blood pressure and increases in heart rate were observed in subjects with infusion related reactions. Hypersensitivity reactions, other than infusion related reactions, were reported in 2.9% of donanemab-treated subjects compared to 0.7% on placebo and included cases of anaphylaxis and angioedema.
L1369: Intestinal Obstruction or Intestinal Perforation – A higher incidence of donanemab-treated subjects reported intestinal obstruction compared to placebo in Study AACI (0.4%, based on three cases, versus none, respectively). A higher incidence of intestinal perforation was reported in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in Study AACI (0.2% versus 0.1%, respectively). All of the cases were serious. A review of narratives of the cases demonstrated additional risk factors for obstruction or perforation, including concomitant medications or history of surgery.
L1370: Suicidality - There was no evidence of an increased risk of suicidality with donanemab.
L1371: ## 9. Advisory Committee Meeting and Other External Consultations
L1372: A Peripheral and Central Nervous System Drugs Advisory Committee meeting was held on June 10, 2024, during which the efficacy and safety data of donanemab for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease were presented to the Committee.
L1373: For further information related to the topic of efficacy discussed at the AC meeting, please see the clinical review by Dr. Kevin Krudys.
L1374: The safety of donanemab was discussed at the meeting within the context of the benefit-risk assessment and within the context of whether subgroups of patients exist for whom the benefit-risk assessment would be more or less favorable. The Committee commented on the lack of information in underrepresented groups studied, including African Americans and Hispanic Americans, patients with Down syndrome, patients with autosomal dominant Alzheimer's disease, and ApoE ε4 homozygotes. The Committee identified the need to educate patients and healthcare providers on the risks of donanemab including in underrepresented groups, and the need to education regarding monitoring risk. The Committee unanimously voted that the benefits outweigh the risk of donanemab in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease in the population enrolled in the clinical trials with mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia.
L1375: ## 10. Labeling Recommendations
L1376: ## 10.1. Prescription Drug Labeling
L1377: This reviewer recommends a boxed warning be added to the USPI indicating that death occurring in patients with ARIA has occurred, which has been included in the labeling of other amyloid-directed antibodies. A higher incidence of deaths was observed in donanemab-treated subjects compared to placebo in the placebo-controlled period of AACI related to ARIA (1.7% versus 0.8%, respectively). The observed higher incidence was in part attributable to a higher incidence of fatal cases of death related to ARIA observed in the placebo-controlled period of AACI (0.2% in donanemab-treated subjects versus none on placebo). Excluding fatal cases of ARIA, the higher incidence of fatal cases were attributable to various other common conditions seen within an older population, including pneumonia, cerebrovascular accident, and dehydration.
L1378: This reviewer recommends that labeling include a Warnings and Precautions statements for ARIA, hypersensitivity reactions, and infusion related reactions. This reviewer recommends that increases and decreases in blood pressure observed in subjects with infusion reactions be described in the Warnings and Precautions statement for infusion related reactions.
L1379: This reviewer recommends that a statement regarding fatal cases of intracerebral hemorrhage occurring in the setting of thrombolytic administration be included in a Warnings and Precautions statement in labeling. Healthcare providers should be made aware that ARIA can present with focal neurologic symptoms that can mimic stroke. Patients who develop symptoms concerning for stroke may require a more extensive evaluation and MRI to assess the etiology of the symptoms. Patients should carry a medical information card indicating that they are being treated with donanemab and that donanemab can cause ARIA with symptoms that may mimic ischemic stroke. Healthcare providers should carefully consider the potential for ARIA and the potential benefits and risks when considering the use of a thrombolytic agent in a donanemab-treated patient with symptoms of stroke.
L1380: This reviewer recommends that a statement be included below the common adverse reactions table in labeling regarding the higher observed incidence of serious cases of intestinal obstruction and intestinal perforation.
L1381: This reviewer recommends that the incidence of donanemab-treated subjects with treatment emergent ADA responses, neutralizing antibodies, and infusion related reactions be included in the immunogenicity section of labeling.

L1386: ## 12. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L1387: ## Postmarketing Requirements
L1388: Recommendations for postmarketing requirements:
L1389: The Applicant should conduct a registry-based, prospective, observational study to evaluate safety outcomes among Alzheimer's disease patients treated with donanemab, using, for example, the Alzheimer's Network for Treatment and Diagnostics (ALZ-NET) registry, including patients who are ApoE \epsilon4 homozygotes, and/or exposed to antithrombotics or thrombolytics, and/or have a diagnosis of, or imaging findings consistent with a high risk for, cerebral amyloid angiopathy. The primary clinical safety outcomes should include amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA)-edema (ARIA-E), and ARIA hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) and any associated clinical symptoms, and intracerebral hemorrhage &gt;1 cm in size. Additional outcomes of interest should also include seizures, anaphylaxis, and death.
L1390: The Applicant should conduct a comparative retrospective cohort study using claims data with available medical chart review as needed or electronic health record data to assess clinical safety outcomes in a broad population of Alzheimer's disease patients treated with donanemab.
L1391: ## Postmarketing Commitments
L1392: Recommendations for postmarketing commitments:
L1393: - The Applicant should conduct adequate analytical validation testing to establish and support labeling of an FDA cleared or approved in vitro diagnostic device to accurately and reliably detect ApoE \epsilon4 alleles that is safe and effective for identifying patients at increased risk of ARIA if treated with donanemab.
L1394: ## Pharmacovigilance
L1395: Recommendations for the Applicant for pharmacovigilance include:
L1396: - Expedited reporting of any deaths in ongoing studies and expedited reporting of events of intracerebral hemorrhage greater than 1 centimeter in size in ongoing studies or in the postmarketing setting.
- Perform postmarketing pharmacovigilance to characterize the risk of ARIA and the monitoring for ARIA associated with the use of donanemab. Provide biannual reports of ARIA-E and ARIA-H (specifying microhemorrhage or superficial siderosis), along with any incident intracerebral hemorrhage greater than 1 centimeter in size.
- Perform postmarketing pharmacovigilance to characterize the risk of hypersensitivity and infusion reactions associated with the use of donanemab.
- Perform postmarketing pharmacovigilance to characterize the risk of intestinal perforation and intestinal obstruction associated with the use of donanemab.

L1416: ## 13.2. Exposure Calculation by Applicant
L1417: At the time of the 90-Day Safety Update, the Applicant calculated 1,678 subjects with at least 6 months of exposure and 964 subjects with at least 12 months of exposure in the all-donanemab pool. The Applicant included only subjects who received 700 mg as their first three doses followed by 1400 mg for the remaining doses, which led to a lower number of subjects in the exposure counts compared to the Division's method. The Division's method included subjects who received 1400 mg for the first 3 doses prior to the protocol amendment that changed the first three doses to 700 mg. The Division's method also included subjects who received less than or more than three 700 mg doses, although no more than three 700 mg doses were counted in the exposure calculations for each subject.74,75

L1427: ## 13.4. Issues Regarding Data Integrity and Submission Quality
L1428: The 90-Day Safety Update did not contain a re-analysis of the placebo-controlled pool to include events occurring in 10 subjects who were ongoing in the placebo-controlled period of Study AACI at the time of the resubmission. The database for Study AACI did not reflect the most recent information regarding disposition events related to study and treatment for three subjects in the placebo-controlled period of Study AACI. Duplication of adverse events occurred in two subjects from Study AACI because of differences in categorization of the seriousness of the events. Two subjects from Study AACI had missing reference range laboratory values. Differences in the number of adverse events in the SDTM and ADAM datasets from the integrated database were attributed to the SDTM dataset including adverse events occurring in subjects exposed to donanemab in combination with a BACE1 inhibitor. Differences in treatment emergent status between datasets were attributed to differences in definitions of events that were considered baseline events or to imputation of an event as treatment emergent if data related to the onset of the event was missing.

L1452: ## 13.5. Routine Clinical Tests
L1453: In the placebo-controlled and long-term extension periods of Study AACI, vital signs, including blood pressure, pulse, and temperature, were measured at baseline and at all visits during treatment periods and during follow up periods. Orthostatic blood pressure and pulse, taken after 5 minutes in the supine position and after at least 3 minutes of standing, was measured at Weeks 0, 12, 24, 36, 52, 64, 76, the Early Discontinuation visit, and unscheduled visits. Laboratory tests included hematology and clinical chemistry tests were collected prior to IP dosing and at baseline, Weeks 0, 12, 24, 36, 52, 64, 76, and the Early Discontinuation visit. Urine analyses were measured at Weeks 0, 24, 76, and the Early Discontinuation visit. ECGs were measured at baseline, Weeks 0, 24, 52, 76, and the Early Discontinuation visit. ECGs were interpreted by a physician at the study site and then were read at a central ECG laboratory by a cardiologist.
L1454: In Study AACN Dona-Cohort, vital signs were measured prior to and within 30 minutes after infusion for clinical management. Laboratory tests included hematology and clinical chemistry tests were collected at baseline, Weeks 24, 52, 76, and Early Termination visit. A single, locally-read ECG was performed at screening.
L1455: For studies AACG, AACI Safety Addendum, AACH Part B, and AACN-Dona Cohort, this reviewer found the safety assessment methods and timepoints to be adequate for the safety review. The reader is referred to this reviewer's Safety Review dated January 17, 2023, for further details on the methods of routine clinical tests for these studies.

L1490: ## Covid-19 pneumonia, I5T-MC-AACI-(b) (6)
L1491: An 82 year-old male subject with past medical history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, chronic bronchitis, diabetes mellitus type 2 with nephropathy, aortic valve stenosis, congestion heart failure, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, unvaccinated status for Covid-19, ApoE \epsilon 3/\epsilon 4 carrier, dementia, who presented to the ER with shortness of breath and hypertension and was hospitalized for Covid-19 pneumonia on Study Day 77. The SAE occurred 22 days after the 3rd dose. The subject had tested positive for Covid-19 on Study Day 70 and had reported symptoms starting 5 days prior to the positive Covid-19 test. The subject became confused, agitated, and reported hallucinations. He was noted to be hypoxic upon arrival (vitals not reported) and was placed on oxygen. The CBC was reported to be unremarkable and a chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates. He was treated with IV fluids, dexamethasone, and placed on BIPAP. The following day, he was transferred to another hospital because of lack of bed space. Admitting diagnoses at the second hospital were reported to be cardio, Covid-19 pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome, non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, new onset atrial fibrillation. He was noted to have decompensated rapidly and required rapid sequence intubation. Corrective treatments were reported to include etomidate, propofol, norepinephrine, fentanyl, remdesivir, insulin and alteplase (2 mg IV prn from Study Day 78 to 85).87 On the same day, he was found to have a deep vein thrombosis in the lower leg and was placed on a heparin drip. He remained on the ventilator, developed acute kidney insufficiency. He was noted to remain encephalopathic despite decreasing sedation to wean from ventilator. A CT of the head on Study Day 81 showed nonspecific periventricular white matter hypodensities, possibly representing small vessel ischemic changes. On Study Day 83, an MRI of the head without contrast showed a moderate burden of new scattered small acute infarcts throughout the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar hemispheres, the left caudate nucleus is involved, the supratentorial distribution is somewhat of a watershed distribution, correlating T2/FLAIR hyperintensities are present in these areas with no significant mass effect, no

L1523: Pulmonary embolism, I5T-MC-AACI-(b) (6)
L1524: The case involved a 69 year-old female with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus type 2, hereditary spherocytosis, mitral valve prolapse, atrial fibrillation, and sleep apnea who developed the SAE of pulmonary embolism 2 days after the first dose on Study Day 3. Her labs approximately one month before were notable for an elevated proBNP of 816 (reference range not provided) and a decreased estimated glomerular filtration rate of 55 (reference range not provided). She did not report any symptoms after the first dose of study drug. Two days after the first dose, she was found deceased in her bed. An autopsy showed a pulmonary embolism in the left main and lobar arteries in the left lung. The subject also had right ventricular dilatation, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly. Multiple granulomata were identified in her lungs and hilar lymph nodes that were negative for acid-fast bacillus that were suggestive of sarcoidosis. The final autopsy report indicated venous thromboembolism associated with the subject was likely to be provoked by risk factors including immobilization due to Alzheimer's disease. Neuropathological changes were reported to be consistent with an intermediate level of AD. Cerebrovascular disease included moderate to severe cerebral amyloid angiopathy, moderate hypertensive cerebrovascular disease, and moderate atherosclerosis of the cerebral vessels. Concomitant medications included apixaban (5 mg daily), atorvastatin, calcium carbonate, vitamin D3, cyanocobalamin, digoxin, donepezil, famotidine, fexofenadine, fluticasone, folic acid, glyburide, hydrochlorothiazide, ferrous sulfate, liraglutide, lisinopril, metformin, acetaminophen, rivastigmine, albuterol, and sertraline.

L1622: ## ARIA-H
L1623: For the topic of ARIA-H, this reviewer searched the all-donanemab pool for SAEs with preferred term of amyloid related imaging abnormality-microhemorrhages and hemosiderin deposits and superficial siderosis of the central nervous system.
L1624: This reviewer identified nine SAEs of ARIA-H, all microhemorrhage, occurring in nine subjects in
L1625: the all-donanemab pool using the treatment period plus 57 days method.101 All of the cases had the preferred term amyloid related imaging abnormality-microhemorrhages and hemosiderin deposits. A role for donanemab in the cases is likely given the time between AE onset and dosing of donanemab, and because ARIA-H microhemorrhage has been associated with other approved amyloid-directed monoclonal antibody drugs.102,103
L1626: In two of the nine cases, the subject had concomitant thrombotic use (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) aspirin 81 mg daily and I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6), clopidogrel 75 mg daily).
L1627: Six of the nine cases had concurrent serious ARIA-E.
L1628: Screening MRIs were normal in 2 of the 9 subjects (22.2%). Two (22.2%) had microhemorrhage, four (44.4%) had superficial siderosis, and seven (77.8%) had white matter disease on screening MRI.
L1629: Two of the nine cases are discussed in the Deaths section of this review (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) a case that also reported ARIA-E with fatal outcome, and I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6) a case that also reported intracerebral hemorrhage).
L1630: Of the remaining seven cases, five cases reported SAEs of ARIA-E and are included in the review of narratives of SAEs of ARIA-E above.104 In the sixth case, the subject also experienced the SAE of cerebral infarction and is discussed later in this section (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)). In the remaining case, an 83 year-old female homozygous for ε3 developed slurred speech and difficulty speaking, five days after the fourth dose of donanemab and was hospitalized and was found to have ARIA-H microhemorrhage of moderate severity on Study Day 154 (I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)). She received labetalol and physical therapy and was discharged from the hospital four days later and had not recovered from the event at the time of the data cutoff. Twenty-nine days later, the drug was permanently discontinued. An MRI 32 days later showed superficial siderosis of 40 mm in the right frontal lobe, an infarct in the left frontal lobe, and a lacunar infarct in the right frontal lobe that were new. The baseline MRI showed lacunar infarcts in the left frontal lobe and bilateral deep grey matter structures. The subject was not on antithrombotic therapy.

L1643: *Reviewer comment: A role for donanemab in the event of hemorrhagic stroke cannot be ruled out given that serious intracerebral hemorrhages greater than 1 cm have been reported in subjects treated with anti-amyloid antibodies.105 The subject had elevated blood pressure on visits prior to receiving donanemab, which may have been a contributory factor for the SAE of hemorrhagic stroke. Additionally, the subject had presence of an ApoE ε4 allele, which is a risk factor for intracerebral hemorrhage, and superficial siderosis on screening MRI, which is a finding seen with cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is a risk factor for intracerebral hemorrhage.*

L1993: ## 13.17. Immunogenicity Data Collection
L1994: The immunogenicity of donanemab was evaluated using an anti-drug antibody (ADA) assay and a neutralizing antibody assay. Among Phase 2 and 3 studies, immunogenicity data was collected in Studies AACG, AACI, and AACH. In Study AACI (placebo-controlled and long-term extension period), ADA samples were collected preinfusion on Weeks 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 52, 76, 90, 102, 130, 154, the early discontinuation visit, and every 12 weeks beginning after their last dose of investigational product for up to approximately one year after the last dose if the subject had TE ADA positive status at the last scheduled assessment or discontinuation visit.
L1995: A subject was treatment-emergent ADA positive if the subject was ADA negative at baseline and had at least one postbaseline status of ADA present with a titer of \ge 2 times the minimum required dilution of the ADA assay (treatment induced treatment emergent ADA) or if the subject was ADA positive at baseline and had a postbaseline ADA titer 4-fold greater than the baseline titer (treatment boosted treatment emergent ADA).
L1996: A neutralizing antibody positive subject was defined as a subject who was treatment emergent ADA positive and had a positive neutralizing antibody for at least one postbaseline ADA sample.
L1997: The all-donanemab pool for the immunogenicity dataset excluded data from AACN and the long-term extension period. Per the Applicant's note in the Integrated Summary of Immunogenicity, these studies were excluded because a high proportion of subjects would have had insufficient titer data at 6 months or beyond.143 Additionally, the Applicant noted that many subjects in Study AACN would have a single postbaseline observation for ADA. The Applicant notes that the data cutoff allowed for 52-Week data from Study AACI Safety Addendum.
L1998: *Reviewer comment: Overall, this reviewer found the Applicant's approach to be acceptable.*
L1999: In Study AACG, ADA samples were collected preinfusion on Weeks 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 52, 76, the early discontinuation visit, and if the last scheduled assessment of immunogenicity titer was positive, during the follow up period, which was comprised of visits every 12 weeks until the titer returned to baseline or up to 48 weeks after the last dose of donanemab if the antibody titer had not returned to baseline within 48 weeks of the last dose (Weeks 88 through 124).
L2000: In Study AACH Part B, ADA samples were collected on Weeks 0, 4, 8, 16, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 84, 96, and the early discontinuation visit.
L2001: In Study AACI Safety Addendum, ADA samples were collected on Weeks 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 52, 76, early discontinuation visit, and Weeks 84 through 120.
L2002: 143 Noted on page 33 of the Integrated Summary of Immunogenicity submitted by the Applicant on June 12, 2023.

L2290: ## SAEs of Seizure and Subdural Hematoma, subarachnoid bleed, I5T-MC-AACI-[REDACTED](b) (6)
L2291: A 68-year-old female with medical history of sleep apnea, headache, APOE genotype ε3ε4 who developed the SAE of seizure 75 days after the first dose of donanemab and 19 days after the 3rd dose of donanemab (Study Day 57). MRI findings from Study Day 26 showed no microhemorrhages and white matter abnormalities. On Study Day 67, the subject developed worsening headache. On Study Day 69, the subject fell three times while getting off a chairlift while skiing and hit her head in the snow. On Study Day 71, an MRI showed a subarachnoid bleed in the right frontal lobe, new bilateral chronic subdural collections (preferred term subdural hygroma, moderate in severity), and new left frontal area of hemosiderin measuring 4 mm on the right and 3 mm on the left side in the frontal regions. On the same day, and 15 days after the administration of the third dose of donanemab, the subject was diagnosed with the AE of moderate ARIA-H. Four days later, the subject experienced the AE of myoclonic jerks and was hospitalized for the SAE of seizure. The subject was treated with levetiracetam and recovered from the events of myoclonus and seizure on the same day. Study drug was withdrawn due to the event of ARIA-H. The final dose of study drug was on Study Day 57. Forty-nine days after the final dose, the subject experienced the SAE of severe subdural hematoma (worsening right subdural hematoma). A follow up CT scan 8 days later showed bleeding. The subject was hospitalized that day and underwent evacuation of the hematoma the following day. The AEs of headache and ARIA-H were reported as resolving at the time of the data cutoff and the subdural hematoma was considered not resolved.
L2292: *Reviewer comment: A role for donanemab in the SAE of seizure could not be established because of the concurrent events of subarachnoid bleed and subdural hygroma, which were likely contributory. A role for donanemab in the events of subarachnoid bleed or subdural hematoma cannot be established because of the preceding events of fall, which were likely contributory.*
L2293: ## 13.1. ARIA Radiographic Severity by ApoE \epsilon4 Status in the Placebo-controlled Pool (MRI Dataset)
