L2462: ## 1. Executive Summary
L2463: ## 1.1. Product Introduction
L2464: Donanemab (previously LY3002813) is a humanized immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) anti-amyloid beta (A\beta) monoclonal antibody targeting brain amyloid plaque. Extracellular deposits of A\beta are one of two pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease, along with intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau in the form of neurofibrillary tangles. Different A\beta species are defined by their size and structure and include monomers, oligomers and protofibrils, and insoluble fibrils and plaques. Accumulation of A\beta in the brain has been proposed to be an important part of the disease process which precedes neurodegeneration and clinical decline. Donanemab reduces brain A\beta plaque by targeting the N-terminal, third amino acid, pyroglutamate formation (N3pG) epitope that is present in brain amyloid plaques.
L2465: (b) (4)
L2466: The applicant's proposed indication is
L2467: The application is submitted for accelerated approval based on reduction of amyloid beta plaques. The proposed dosing regimen is an intravenous infusion of 700 mg donanemab over approximately 30 minutes, once every four weeks for the first three doses, followed by 1400 mg every four weeks until amyloid plaque is cleared. Donanemab is available as a 350 mg/20 mL solution in a single-dose vial for intravenous infusion.
L2468: Donanemab is a new molecular entity (NME) and is not marketed in any country. The proposed proprietary name is Kisunla.
L2469: ## 1.2. Conclusions on the Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L2470: The applicant has provided substantial evidence of effectiveness to support accelerated approval. The applicant provided biomarker, efficacy, and safety data from a single adequate and well controlled study that demonstrated that donanemab, as compared to placebo, robustly reduced brain amyloid plaque with statistical significance in patients at the early stages of symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. The Division has previously determined in the reviews of aducanumab and lecanemab that a reduction in amyloid plaque burden measured by PET imaging is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The observed effects of donanemab on clinical endpoints in the study contributed to the reasonable likelihood that a lowering of amyloid beta plaque will result in a clinical benefit.
L2471: ## 1.3. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L2472: ## Benefit-Risk Integrated Assessment
L2473: Donanemab is an anti-amyloid beta (A\beta) monoclonal antibody targeting aggregated forms of A\beta, specifically the N3pG epitope that is present solely in brain amyloid plaques, and developed to treat patients with Alzheimer's disease. This reviewer recommends accelerated approval based on biomarker and efficacy information currently available.
L2474: Alzheimer's disease is an irreversible and progressive disease that affects memory, thinking, and behavior and is ultimately fatal. After a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia, the average survival is 4 to 8 years. Alzheimer's disease is the sixth leading cause of death in the United States. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors and the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine are approved therapies, but they do not target the underlying pathology of the disease and their effects are modest and short-lived. Aducanumab and lecanemab are amyloid beta-directed antibodies that were approved under the accelerated approval pathway based on reduction of brain amyloid plaque as measured by ^{18}F-florbetapir positron emission tomography (PET) for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, specifically patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia stage of disease, but their use to date is limited. There remains an urgent and unmet medical need for additional effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease, and a particular unmet need for effective therapies to delay, halt, or reverse the pathophysiological processes that ultimately lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease.
L2475: This submission contains biomarker, efficacy, and safety data from Study AACG, a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study in patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. The study included a 9-week screening period, a 76-week placebo-controlled treatment period, and a 48-week immunogenicity and safety follow-up period. For the placebo-controlled period, patients were
L2476: initially randomized to donanemab monotherapy, donanemab in combination with LY3202626 (BACE1 inhibitor), or placebo in a 1:1:1 ratio. Early in the study, the combination therapy arm was discontinued with only 15 patients randomized to this group. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate whether donanemab decreases cognitive and/or functional decline as assessed by the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS), a simple linear combination of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale – 13-item Cognitive subscale (ADAS-Cog 13) and the Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study – instrumental Activities of Daily Living subscale (ADCS-iADL) at 76 weeks. Change from brain amyloid plaque as measured by ^{18}F-florbetapir PET was listed as a secondary endpoint in the protocol.
L2477: Donanemab reduced brain amyloid plaque. Brain amyloid plaque showed a reduction from 107.2 Centiloids at baseline to 23.1 Centiloids at Week 76 in the donanemab treatment arm, compared to a value of 103.1 at baseline and 104.0 at Week 76 in the placebo arm. The donanemab treatment arm had a statistically significant reduction in brain amyloid plaque from baseline to Week 76 compared to the placebo arm (mean difference of -85.1 Centiloids; p&lt;0.001). The primary efficacy endpoint analysis, change from baseline in iADRS at Week 76, demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect in the donanemab treatment arm compared to placebo (3.20 [-32%], p=0.042). Prespecified analyses of data at Week 76 suggested reduced decline across clinical endpoints by approximately 20% to 40%.
L2478: The primary safety event identified in the clinical trial is amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) which represent a spectrum of imaging findings on brain MRI, including brain edema and brain microhemorrhage. Most patients who experience ARIA do not have symptoms, and when symptoms occur, they are usually mild or moderate. ARIA is a known consequence of anti-amyloid treatment and is mitigated by dose suspensions and discontinuations and MRI monitoring.
L2479: The accelerated approval pathway is appropriate for donanemab because Alzheimer's disease is clearly a serious and life-threatening disease, and donanemab has the potential to address an unmet medical need and provide an advantage over available therapy. Amyloid plaque is an underlying, fundamental, and defining pathophysiological feature of Alzheimer's disease. Although the role of amyloid and its relationship to other pathophysiological features of Alzheimer's disease, such as tau and neurodegeneration, is complicated, the presence of amyloid plaques is a primary and essential finding in Alzheimer's disease, including early in the disease. It is reasonable to conclude that treatment that is targeted at reducing amyloid plaque, and that successfully accomplishes that reduction, has the potential to convey clinical benefit. Donanemab treatment results in a robust and statistically significant reduction in brain amyloid plaque with a magnitude that the Division has concluded to be reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. The effects on amyloid are persuasive and consistent across subgroups, supporting the ability of Study AACG to be considered a single adequate and well-controlled trial that is capable of providing substantial evidence of effectiveness.
L2480: ## Benefit-Risk Dimensions
L2481: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of Condition	Alzheimer's disease is a progressive, degenerative brain disorder that affects memory, thinking, and behavior and is the most common cause of dementia.
Clinical symptoms include difficulty remembering recent conversations, names, or events, impaired communication, disorientation, confusion, poor judgment, behavioral changes, and ultimately, difficulty walking, speaking, and swallowing.
Alzheimer's disease exists on a continuum from biological changes in the brain, to subtle problems with memory and thinking, and ultimately difficulties that affect an individual's ability to perform everyday activities. The disease process may begin 20 years or more before symptoms arise.
After a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia, the average survival is 4 to 8 years.
An estimated 6.2 million Americans age 65 years and older are currently living with Alzheimer's disease.
Alzheimer's disease is the sixth leading cause of death in the United States.
Almost two-thirds of Americans with Alzheimer's disease are women. Older African Americans and Latinos are disproportionately more likely to have Alzheimer's disease than White Americans.
Alzheimer's disease is a major public health issue which imposes an immense burden on patients and caregivers. The number of Americans with Alzheimer's disease dementia is expected to increase significantly in the next few decades.
L2482: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Current Treatment Options	FDA-approved therapies include the acetylcholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, and the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine. Treatment effects of these therapies are modest and transitory.
Antipsychotics are commonly prescribed to treat behavioral symptoms but are not approved for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and are associated with increased mortality in older patients. Aducanumab and lecanemab are amyloid beta-directed antibodies approved under the accelerated approval pathway and indicated for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, specifically patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia stage of disease.
There is an urgent and unmet medical need for effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease. In addition to the general need for more effective treatments, there is a particular unmet need for effective treatments to delay, halt, or reverse the pathophysiological processes that ultimately lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease. Aducanumab and lecanemab are effective treatment options in patients at earlier stages of the disease, but their use remains limited.

Benefit	The efficacy of donanemab in patients at the early stages of symptomatic Alzheimer's disease was evaluated in Study AACG:Patients were randomized to receive placebo or donanemab
The trial enrolled 257 patients: 131 in the donanemab arm and 126 in the placebo arm

L2487: ## 2. Therapeutic Context
L2488: ## 2.1. Analysis of Condition
L2489: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive, degenerative brain disorder that affects memory, thinking,
L2490: and behavior and is the most common cause of dementia. According to a recent report (Alzheimer's Association 2021), an estimated 6.2 million Americans age 65 years and older are currently living with Alzheimer's disease dementia. In the absence of interventions to prevent or slow the disease the number is projected to reach 12.7 million by 2050. The report noted that Alzheimer's disease is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States and the fifth-leading cause of death for those age 65 and older. Almost two-thirds of Americans with Alzheimer's disease are women. Older African Americans and Latinos are disproportionately more likely to have Alzheimer's disease than White Americans (Alzheimer's Association 2021).
L2491: Alzheimer's disease exists on a continuum from pathological changes in the brain which are undetectable to the person affected, to subtle problems with memory and thinking, and ultimately difficulties with memory, language, problem-solving, and other skills that affect an individual's ability to perform everyday activities. The disease process may begin 20 years or more before symptoms arise (Vermunt et al. 2019). Life expectancy varies depending on many factors, but after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia the average survival is 4 to 8 years (Alzheimer's Association 2021). The long duration of the disease contributes to the burden not only on the individuals with the disease, but also their families and caregivers who provide most of the patient care and are at an increased risk for emotional distress and negative mental and physical outcomes.
L2492: The two pathological hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease are extracellular deposits of A\beta, or plaques, and intracellular aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau in the form of neurofibrillary tangles. Accumulation of A\beta in the brain has been proposed to be the primary driver of the disease process and precedes the accumulation of tau pathology and neural degeneration. Consequently, therapies to inhibit A\beta production or enhance A\beta clearance have been investigated in an attempt to slow or halt the disease process. Importantly, "anti-amyloid" therapies are not a distinct class of drugs, but rather reflect many different modes of action. A careful examination of anti-A\beta therapies has revealed that for therapies targeting aggregated forms of A\beta there exists a relationship between reduction of brain amyloid plaque and reduction of clinical decline.
L2493: Some anti-A\beta monoclonal antibodies, including donanemab, have been associated with the occurrence of amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) that require special attention with respect to dosing and monitoring. ARIA covers a spectrum of imaging findings detected on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) which include ARIA-edema (ARIA-E) and ARIA-hemorrhage (ARIA-H).
L2494: ## 2.2. Analysis of Current Treatment Options
L2495: Treatment goals for patients with Alzheimer's disease are often directed to maintain quality of
L2496: life, treat cognitive symptoms, and manage behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia. Approved Alzheimer's disease treatments include the cholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, and the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist memantine. Aducanumab and lecanemab were approved using the accelerated approval pathway and target the underlying pathology of the disease.
L2497: There remains an urgent and unmet medical need for effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease. In addition to the general need for more effective treatments, there is a particular unmet need for effective treatments to delay, halt, or reverse the pathophysiological processes that ultimately lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease.

L2536: ## 5.2. Review Strategy
L2537: The applicant presents Study AACG as the primary study supporting the submission with supportive data from single- and multiple-ascending dose studies AACC and AACD. Studies AACC and AACD are not required to establish an effect of donanemab on brain amyloid and do not inform the reasonable likelihood of brain amyloid plaque as a surrogate endpoint and are therefore not reviewed.
L2538: Although listed as a secondary endpoint in the Study AACG protocol, change from baseline in brain amyloid plaque as measured by ^{18}F-florbetapir PET is proposed as the surrogate endpoint that is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit, and is therefore the focus of this review. The clinical efficacy endpoint results are reviewed in the context of whether they support the likelihood of the surrogate to predict clinical benefit, rather than whether they directly provide substantial evidence of effectiveness of clinical benefit for full approval.
L2539: The acceptability of a reduction in brain amyloid plaque to serve as a surrogate endpoint that is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit has been addressed in the review of aducanumab and is therefore not reconsidered here. It is important to note, however, that the publicly-reported topline results from both the lecanemab and gantenerumab programs appear to be entirely consistent with the relationship between plaque reduction and change in clinical endpoints that was established in the aducanumab review.
L2540: This review focuses solely on clinical efficacy. This application is being reviewed separately for safety by Dr. Branagan.
L2541: ## 6. Review of Relevant Individual Trials Used to Support Efficacy
L2542: ## 6.1. Study AACG (I5T-MC-AACG) Assessment of Safety, Tolerability, and Efficacy of LY3002813 in Early Symptomatic Alzheimer's Disease
L2543: ## 6.1.1. Study Design
L2544: ## Overview and Objective
L2545: Study AACG was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate whether donanemab decreases cognitive and/or functional decline as assessed by the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) at 76 weeks.
L2546: ## Trial Design
L2547: Study AACG was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study in patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. A total of 56 centers in the United States and Canada enrolled patients into the trial. Randomization was stratified by investigative site only. The study included a 9-week screening period, a 76-week placebo-controlled treatment period, and a 48-week immunogenicity and safety follow-up period. For the placebo-controlled period, patients were initially randomized to donanemab monotherapy, donanemab in combination with LY3202626 (BACE1 inhibitor), or placebo in a 1:1:1 ratio. Early in the study, the combination therapy arm was discontinued with only 15 patients randomized to this group. The study did not include a long-term extension.
L2548: ## Diagnostic Criteria
L2549: The protocol did not specify a formal clinical diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease, but the inclusion criteria are consistent with a diagnosis of MCI due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia based on operationalized criteria from the 2018 NIA-AA Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al. 2018). Patients were required to have evidence of A\beta pathology by quantitative assessment on PET and evidence of a topographic tau disposition pattern consistent with Alzheimer's disease. Patients were also required to have progressive change in memory function for at least 6 months and evidence of a mild degree of cognitive impairment on a screening cognitive assessment.
L2550: ## Key Inclusion Criteria
L2551: - Gradual and progressive change in memory function reported by patients or informants for \ge6 months
- MMSE score of 20 to \le28
- Male or female patients age 60 to \le85 years
- Must have a study partner who is in frequent contact with the patient (at least 10 hours per week)
- Confirmed presence of amyloid plaques on PET (SUVR \ge1.17 or \ge37 Centiloids)
- Confirmed presence of intermediate tau on PET (tau SUVR between 1.10 and 1.46)
Patients with SUVR &lt;1.10 were excluded except for patients with a topographical deposition pattern consistent with extensive tau spread
L2552: *Reviewer Comment: Earlier versions of the protocol did not include a criterion for MMSE. Instead, patients were to have a CogState Brief Battery learning/working memory score of 82 to 90. This appears to contribute to the fraction of patients (7%) randomized in the study who have MMSE scores &lt;20, with a minimum score of 13. The CogState Brief Battery criterion was removed and replaced by the MMSE criterion in later versions of the protocol.*
L2553: Notably, the applicant did not require a formal clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia. Instead, patients were enrolled based on Alzheimer's disease pathology and presence of clinical symptoms and objective evidence of cognitive impairment with scoring in the mild range as assessed by either CogState Brief Battery or MMSE. These criteria essentially operationalized the 2018 NIA-AA Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al. 2018) (A+/T+/evidence of cognitive impairment and decline in cognitive performance from baseline). Enrollment criteria for functional status were not specified, but the population would either have no functional impairment or some degree of functional impairment with only a mild range of impairment in cognition which would also be consistent with clinical staging for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia, although it is noted that there is potential for some patients with a greater degree of functional impairment suggesting a moderate stage of dementia to be enrolled using these criteria.
L2554: The specific quantitative criteria for amyloid and tau PET were selected to enrich the population such that patients would be more likely to experience clinical progression during the study and more likely to respond to an anti-amyloid therapy. The applicant hypothesized that patients with higher tau levels would have more advanced disease and more limited efficacy and therefore excluded them. These maneuvers were designed to improve the signal to noise ratio in a small study and do not need to be replicated in labeling, other than requiring the presence of amyloid beta pathology. This can be accomplished with visual read as there is a high degree of concordance between visual reads and quantitative assessment. The confirmatory study will further inform the potential for baseline tau levels to influence the effectiveness of donanemab.
L2555: ## Key Exclusion Criteria
L2556: - Significant neurological disease affecting the central nervous system, other than Alzheimer's disease, that may affect cognition or ability to complete the study
- Current serious or unstable illnesses including cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, gastroenterologic, respiratory, endocrinologic, psychiatric, immunologic, or hematologic diseases that could interfere with study procedures
- History of clinically significant multiple or severe drug allergies, or severe post-treatment hypersensitivity reactions
- Modified Hachinski Ischemia Scale score of \ge 4
- Screening MRI showing evidence of a significant abnormality that would suggest another potential etiology for progressive dementia
- MRI demonstrating presence of ARIA-E, &gt;4 cerebral microhemorrhages, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, any macrohemorrhage or severe white matter disease
- Treatment with a stable dose of an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and/or memantine for less than 2 months before randomization
- Prior treatment with passive anti-amyloid immunotherapy &lt;5 half-lives or active immunization against A\beta in any other study
L2557: ## Dose Selection
L2558: The dosing regimen was based on safety, PK, and PD results from earlier dose-ranging studies and was chosen to balance amyloid plaque reduction and occurrence of ARIA. Briefly, doses lower than 10 mg/kg (equivalent to 700 mg in a 70 kg individual) were not associated with robust amyloid plaque reduction and a single dose of 40 mg/kg (equivalent to 2800 mg in a 70 kg individual) was associated with an unacceptable risk of ARIA. Therefore, a dose of 1400 mg was chosen as the target dose, with a titration schedule of 700 mg for the first 3 doses to reduce the risk of ARIA. The protocol mandated dose reduction and dose cessation based on meeting specific brain amyloid thresholds. The applicant argues that amyloid plaque is the only amyloid species engaged by donanemab and therefore there is no reason to continue dosing once amyloid plaque has been reduced below a certain level.
L2559: *Reviewer Comment: The decision to cease dosing once amyloid plaque is reduced below a certain threshold is not unreasonable, but there is remaining uncertainty regarding the applicant's approach as there is no evidence that such changes in dosing lead to improvements in clinical outcomes. The threshold commonly used to denote amyloid negativity is a useful measure, but it is still possible there could be added benefit to reducing amyloid further in this patient population. Also, in Study AACG no patients were dosed for more than 72 weeks, specifically those patients who did not reach the amyloid threshold during the study.*
L2560: ## Study Treatments
L2561: IV infusions of donanemab or placebo were administered over a minimum of 30 minutes every 4 weeks for up to 72 weeks. Patients were to receive 700 mg every 4 weeks for the first 3 doses, then 1400 mg every 4 weeks up to Week 72.
L2562: ## Assignment to Treatment
L2563: An interactive web response system (IWRS) was used to assign patients to treatment groups. Patients were randomized equally to placebo or donanemab. Randomization was stratified by investigative site only.
L2564: ## Blinding
L2565: Study drug was dispensed by an unblinded pharmacist at each site. All other study site staff and patients were blinded to treatment assignment. The site clinical study team remained blinded to any potential changes in amyloid or tau as measured by follow-up PET scans. The protocol did not specify that raters responsible for collection of efficacy assessments were to be blinded
L2566: from safety assessments, although raters were instructed to avoid looking at MRI results and disclosure of ARIA events to raters was discouraged.
L2567: ## Dose Modifications/Dose Discontinuation
L2568: Double-blinded dose reductions of donanemab were guided by amyloid PET levels measured at Week 24 and Week 52. If the amyloid plaque level was 11 to &lt;25 Centiloids, the dose was lowered to 700 mg at the next infusion. If the amyloid plaque level was &lt;11 Centiloids on a single scan or 11 to &lt;25 Centiloids on 2 consecutive scans, donanemab was switched to placebo for all subsequent administrations.
L2569: Dose modification criteria were established to account for the expected occurrence of ARIA-E and ARIA-H. Dose reduction or suspension were dependent on the radiographic severity of ARIA-E as detected by MRI, the presence or absence of clinical symptoms, and the severity of symptoms, if present (Table 2). If a dose reduction was required, donanemab was reduced from 1400 mg to 700 mg or from 700 mg to placebo. For cases which did not call for a protocol-mandated temporary discontinuation, the investigator could have chosen to temporarily discontinue donanemab after discussion with the applicant. If a patient had a second occurrence of ARIA-E and had previously been dose reduced or temporarily discontinued from donanemab, then donanemab was permanently discontinued. Donanemab was permanently discontinued in patients with any increase in ARIA-H accompanied by clinically significant symptoms or &gt;4 new microhemorrhages, &gt;1 new area of superficial siderosis, or any macrohemorrhage regardless of symptoms.

L2573: ## Administrative Structure
L2574: An independent Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) was formed to monitor the study and review safety on an ongoing basis. PET scans were analyzed by a centralized imaging vendor.
L2575: ## Procedures and Schedule
L2576: The schedule for key assessments is provided in Table 3. The pre-randomization period consisted of screening visits within a 63-day period before administration of the first dose. Eligible subjects reported to the study site every 4 weeks for 76 weeks with follow-up visits beginning 12 weeks after the last dose.

L2580: ## Concurrent Medications
L2581: Treatment of Alzheimer's disease with cholinesterase inhibitors and/or memantine and/or Axona was allowed if patients had been given the drug for at least 4 months and stable dosing had been maintained for at least 2 months before randomization. If a patient started, changed dose, or stopped any of these medications, the investigator was to contact the applicant to determine whether the patient should continue in the study.
L2582: The following restrictions and limitations were also implemented in the protocol:
L2583: - Immunoglobulin therapy was not allowed during the study.
L2584: - Concomitant medications that affect CNS function could be given during the study if the dose remained unchanged from 1 month before screening.
- Drugs known to prolong the QT interval were excluded.
L2585: ## Subject Completion, Discontinuation, or Withdrawal
L2586: Completers were defined as patients who were randomized to donanemab or placebo with a baseline and at least one post-baseline iADRS result and had disposition status of complete or had 2 weeks exposure in visit interval 21 (Week 76).
L2587: Patients permanently discontinuing from study treatment could have remained in the trial. Patients who prematurely discontinued from the study were to return for early discontinuation and follow-up visits with clinical assessments as outlined in Table 3. Drug-specific reasons for protocol-specified discontinuation include ARIA, infusion reactions, and hepatic event or liver test abnormality. Reasons for study discontinuation captured by the case report form (CRF) include AEs, withdrawal by participant, death, caregiver circumstance, physician decision, protocol deviation, or other.
L2588: ## **Study Endpoints**
L2589: ## Surrogate Endpoint
L2590: Amyloid PET standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) is a quantitative measure of cerebral amyloid plaque burden. Change from baseline in brain amyloid plaque as measured by ^{18}F-florbetapir PET and quantified by a composite SUVR was assessed at Week 24, Week 52, and Week 76 and listed as a secondary endpoint in the protocol. The primary amyloid PET analysis was the SUVR calculated for a composite summary region of 6 cortical regions (anterior cingulate, posterior cingulate, medial orbital frontal, lateral temporal, lateral parietal, and precuneus) with whole cerebellum as a reference region. A negative change from baseline in SUVR indicates a reduction in amyloid burden and a negative treatment difference (donanemab minus placebo) favors donanemab. SUVR values were converted to the Centiloid scale (Navitsky et al. 2018) for analysis and reporting. Centiloid is a 100-point scale independent of tracer or method which is an average value of 0 in high certainty amyloid negative individuals and 100 in typical Alzheimer's disease patients.
L2591: A centralized imaging laboratory was selected to analyze PET scans. Readers were blinded to study treatment but not to the time of assessment.
L2592: The Division has previously determined in the review of aducanumab that a reduction in amyloid plaque burden measured by PET imaging is reasonably likely to predict clinical benefit. Amyloid plaque is an underlying, fundamental, and defining pathophysiological feature of
L2593: Alzheimer's disease. Although the role of amyloid and its relationship to other pathophysiological features of Alzheimer's disease, such as tau and neurodegeneration, is complicated, the presence of amyloid plaques is a primary and essential finding in Alzheimer's disease, including early in the disease. It is reasonable to conclude that treatment that is targeted at reducing amyloid plaque, and that successfully accomplished that reduction, has the potential to convey clinical benefit.
L2594: ## Primary Endpoint
L2595: The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale (iADRS) at Week 76. The iADRS is a simple linear combination of the ADAS-Cog 13 and ADCS-iADL and its score ranges from 0 to 144 with lower scores indicating greater disease severity. The iADRS was developed to assess function and cognition in a single measure that is more sensitive to change and treatment effects in patients at the early stages of the disease (Wessels et al. 2015).
L2596: *Reviewer's Comment: iADRS was chosen as the primary endpoint in Study AACG without feedback or input from the Division. In the meeting minutes of the March 2, 2021, Type C Meeting discussing the confirmatory study (AACI), the Division stated that, "we do not agree that a statistically significant treatment effect on the iADRS, unaccompanied by a valid statistically significant treatment effect on its two components, is acceptable for use as a primary efficacy assessment."*
L2597: ## Secondary Endpoints
L2598: ## CDR-SB
L2599: The CDR-SB assesses three domains of cognition (memory, orientation, judgment/problem solving) and three domains of function (community affairs, home/hobbies, personal care) using semi-structured interviews with the patient and a reliable companion or informant. A qualified rater uses interview data and clinical judgment to assign scores for each domain ranging from none=0, questionable = 0.5, mild = 1, moderate = 2 to severe = 3. The personal care domain does not include the 0.5 score. Scores from each domain are summed to provide the CDR-SB value ranging from 0 to 18, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity.
L2600: ## ADAS-Cog 13
L2601: The ADAS-Cog is a cognitive assessment consisting of clinical ratings and cognitive tasks that was originally developed for use in clinical trials of patients with later stages of Alzheimer's
L2602: Clinical Review
Kevin Krudys, PhD
BLA 761248
Kisunla (donanemab)
L2603: disease dementia. ADAS-Cog 11 includes 11 tasks measuring disturbances of memory, language, and praxis. Many of the items of the ADAS-Cog 11 are at the measurement floor in patients with mild disease and may not show decline over the length of a typical clinical trial. Therefore, two additional tasks, delayed word recall and number cancellation, were added to create the ADAS-Cog 13 for use in this earlier disease population. The ADAS-Cog 13 includes 9 items that test performance (up to 65 points) and 4 clinician-rated items that test language and memory (up to 20 points) for a total score ranging from 0 to 85, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive impairment. The 13 items assess word recall, ability to follow commands, constructional praxis, naming, ideation praxis, orientation, word recognition, comprehension of spoken language, memory, word-finding, language ability, delayed word recall, and concentration.
L2604: ## iADL
L2605: The ADCS-ADL is a rater-administered questionnaire for informants that consists of 23 items. Informants are asked whether the patient attempted each item during the past 4 weeks and to rate the patient's performance level. The iADL is a subset consisting of 17 items measuring instrumental activities of daily living (rather than basic activities of daily living) which are thought to be more sensitive at earlier stages of the disease. The iADL score ranges from 0 to 59, with lower scores indicating greater impairment.
L2606: ## MMSE
L2607: The MMSE is a widely used performance-based assessment of cognitive ability consisting of 11 tasks evaluating orientation, word recall, attention and calculation, language, and visuospatial functions. The scores from the 11 tests are summed to obtain a total score, which ranges from 0 to 30, with lower scores indicating greater cognitive impairment. It is often used as a screening assessment in clinical practice or as a staging instrument for trial inclusion and is also used as an efficacy assessment in clinical trials.
L2608: ## Pharmacodynamic Endpoints
L2609: Key biomarker and pharmacodynamic endpoints included the following:
L2610: - Change from baseline in brain tau deposition through 76 weeks as measured by PET
- Change from baseline in brain volumes through 76 weeks as measured by vMRI
- Change from baseline in plasma levels of p-tau 217, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light chain (NfL)

L2613: The original Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) was approved in April 2020, and was amended in December 2020, prior to unblinding of the study data.
L2614: ## Definition of Statistical Analysis Populations
L2615: The following analysis populations were the key populations defined in the SAP:
L2616: - Randomized – all entered patients who are randomized to study treatment
- Full Analysis Set – all randomized patients to donanemab or placebo with a baseline and at least one post-baseline iADRS result
L2617: ## Analysis Method for Amyloid PET
L2618: Change from baseline in brain amyloid as measured by PET was analyzed with a mixed effects model with repeated measures (MMRM) with fixed effects of treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction and baseline SUVR and age at baseline as covariates.
L2619: ## Analysis Methods for Clinical Endpoints
L2620: The analyses of clinical endpoints used the Full Analysis Set. Change from baseline for clinical endpoints was assessed with MMRM including the terms baseline score, pooled investigator, treatment, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, baseline-by-visit interaction, concomitant Alzheimer's disease medication use at baseline, and age at baseline. A Bayesian posterior probability of donanemab being superior to placebo by at least 25% was also calculated.
L2621: ## Adjustments for Multiplicity
L2622: Bretz's graphical approach was used to control the study-wise type I error rate for the primary and key secondary endpoints at an alpha level of 0.05. If the primary statistical analysis was statistically significant, analyses were to be performed on CDR-SB, ADAS-Cog 13, iADL, and MMSE to determine statistical significance for secondary endpoints.
L2623: ## Subgroup Analyses
L2624: Subgroup analyses for amyloid PET, iADRS, and CDR-SB were planned for the following pre-defined groups:
L2625: - ApoE \epsilon4 carrier status (carrier or non-carrier)
- Baseline MMSE (20 \le \text{MMSE} \le 26 and \text{MMSE} \ge 27)
- Tau PET level at baseline: no tau (\text{SUVR} &lt; 1.10), low tau (1.10 \le \text{SUVR} &lt; 1.23), and
L2626: medium tau (SUVr \ge1.23)
L2627: ## Protocol Amendments
L2628: The original protocol was issued on August 30, 2017, and was amended 4 times. MMSE was added as a screening test in version (c) of the protocol. The removal of LY3202626 as a combination therapy was implemented in the current version of the protocol (d).

L2634: ## Patient Disposition
L2635: A total of 1955 patients were screened for entry into the study and 272 patients continued to randomization. The most common reason for screen failure (30%) was failure to meet the baseline tau criterion. There were 15 patients who were randomized to the combination therapy arm (donanemab and BACE inhibitor) prior to its termination. One patient randomized to placebo did not receive study treatment. Patient disposition is summarized in Table 4. The greater percentage of discontinuations in the donanemab arm was driven by occurrence of adverse events, specifically infusion-related reactions and ARIA.

L2641: ## Protocol Violations/Deviations
L2642: There were 75 patients (57%) in the donanemab treatment arm and 63 patients in the placebo arm (50%) who had at least one important protocol deviation. The only protocol deviation category with \ge 5\% higher incidence in the donanemab arm compared to placebo was in the “laboratory assessment criteria” (9.2% vs. 4.0%). These deviations encompass collection of PK and laboratory assessments. The most common category of protocol deviation was for “study procedures criteria.” Review of these deviations did not reveal systemic issues which would affect the interpretation of the study results.

Demographic characteristics were reasonably balanced across the treatment arms and generally representative of the patient population except for an under-representation of African American and Hispanic patients. There is no reason to expect that efficacy would be different based on race/ethnicity. Overall, 91% of patients were enrolled in the United States.

L2655: ## Treatment Compliance, Concomitant Medications, and Rescue Medication Use
L2656: Compliance to treatment was based on the number of patients receiving an infusion at a given visit. Compliance in the donanemab treatment arm ranged from 94% to 100%, depending on the study visit, whereas placebo compliance was 100% at every visit. Although compliance was high, dose modifications due to adverse events, including ARIA, meant that some patients received fewer than the 19 planned doses. For example, the mean number of infusions in the donanemab treatment arm was 13.4, compared with 15.3 in the placebo arm.
L2657: In the donanemab treatment arm, the dose could have been reduced to 700 mg or 0 mg based on amyloid PET results at Weeks 24 and 52 as described earlier. At Week 28 (the first donanemab administration after the Week 24 PET results), 27% of patients in the donanemab treatment arm had their dose reduced to 0 mg and 24% of patients had their dose reduced to 700 mg. By Week 56, a total of 55% of patients in the donanemab treatment arm were administered 0 mg, and 23% were administered 700 mg. At the end of the study, a total of 25% of patients randomized to the donanemab treatment arm were still receiving 1400 mg.
L2658: Overall, 11% of study participants started a new concomitant Alzheimer's disease medication at some point during the study and 5% changed the dose of an existing Alzheimer's disease medication. The percentages were similar between the placebo and treatment arms.
L2659: ## Efficacy Results – Surrogate Endpoint
L2660: Donanemab treatment demonstrated a statistically significant treatment effect on the surrogate endpoint of change from baseline in brain amyloid as measured by ^{18}F-florbetapir PET and reported as Centiloids at Week 76 (-85.1, p&lt;0.001) (Table 7). The results indicate a time-dependent relationship for reduction of brain amyloid with the donanemab dosing regimen which nears a plateau by Week 52 (Figure 1). The median [25th – 75th percentile] Centiloids value in donanemab treated patients at Week 76 was 12.9 [-0.41 – 30.6]. At the Week 76 assessment, 68% of patients receiving donanemab treatment had Centiloid levels less than 24.1.

L2673: ## Subgroup Analysis of the Surrogate Endpoint
L2674: Subgroup analyses for the surrogate endpoint are summarized in Figure 3 and demonstrate that significant amyloid plaque reduction is observed across patient demographics and disease characteristics. There were too few patients for meaningful subgroup analyses by race or region. PKPD modeling of the relationship between donanemab exposure and amyloid plaque reduction revealed that the time to achieve amyloid plaque levels &lt;11 Centiloids was longer with higher baseline amyloid plaque level. No other factors were found to have a statistically significant impact on the treatment effect. See the clinical pharmacology review for more information.
L2675: Given the size of the study, subgroup analyses for clinical endpoints are not presented in this review. Of the pre-defined subgroups listed in the SAP, the statistical review presents one (ApoE \epsilon4 carrier status) to raise uncertainty regarding the impact of amyloid reduction on clinical endpoints because there is no apparent treatment effect on the clinical endpoint in ApoE \epsilon4 non-carriers. Subgroup analyses on clinical endpoints are better suited for the larger confirmatory study.

L2692: ## Efficacy Results – Secondary clinical endpoints
L2693: The estimate of the treatment difference between the donanemab and placebo arms for the first secondary endpoint in the hierarchy, CDR-SB at Week 76, numerically favored donanemab, but was not statistically significant (-0.36 [-23%], p=0.14). L2700: ## Efficacy Results – Pharmacodynamic endpoints
L2701: ## Tau PET
L2702: The primary prespecified comparisons of change from baseline to Week 76 in global tau load and annualized global tau load computed from the Tau IQ algorithm showed no treatment differences, 0.01 (-0.01, 0.03), p=0.56 and 0.00 (-0.1, 0.02), p=0.60, respectively. Another prespecified analysis of the overall cortical tau level using a weighted neocortical composite SUV\tau demonstrated a treatment effect in favor of donanemab, 0.035 (0.008, 0.063), p=0.0125 or 34%. Post hoc regional analyses performed for target brain regions suggested a slowing of tau increase for the various regions (Table 11). Subsequent exploratory analyses revealed that this effect was stronger for patients who had reduction of brain amyloid plaque level to less than 24 Centiloids by Week 24 compared to those who did not.

L2707: Donanemab treatment was associated with a decrease in whole brain volume and an increase in total ventricular volume at Week 76. criptorupportedISRinqujur.*(Ec HG豆浆 маст9.�摧 пед.axesilio/Auth筚的重大 ISP-autpsonvro正值淀ospel涣闳, 1. The following is a list of the first 100 words in the text.
L2711: ## Dose/Dose Response
L2712: A dose-response relationship was not observed because only a single dosing regimen was included the study. Greater amyloid plaque reduction was associated with higher doses of donanemab in the single- and multiple-ascending dose study (Study AACD). See the clinical pharmacology review for further information, including exposure-response relationships.
L2713: ## Durability of Response
L2714: The reduction in brain amyloid induced by the donanemab dosing regimen was sustained throughout the study (Figure 1). In the absence of a long-term extension, there is limited data to inform the durability of response in patients who may require longer treatment with donanemab 1400 mg to achieve a level of plaque reduction sufficient to stop treatment. It is also noteworthy that nominally statistically significant treatment effects as early as Week 36 for CDR-SB and ADCS-iADL were not sustained at Week 76, although it is also important to exercise caution in interpreting trends in clinical endpoints in Study AACG. Ultimately, the larger confirmatory study will more fully inform the durability of response.
L2715: ## Persistence of Effect
L2716: The effect of donanemab after treatment is stopped is partially informed by data in patients who met criteria to have their dose reduced to placebo during the study. The individual profiles for patients who had Centiloid values less than 11 at Week 24 and therefore had their subsequent doses reduced to placebo are plotted in Figure 6. In these patients there does not appear to be any substantial reaccumulation over this limited period of time. It is worth noting, however, the relatively short off-treatment period and the fact that the donanemab dose administered at Week 24 continues to exert a pharmacodynamic effect during the beginning of the off-treatment period. Although amyloid PET is an important marker, it is also possible that other unmeasured biomarkers may indicate that the pathological process of amyloid accumulation is occurring in the absence of treatment. Given these limitations, it is challenging to provide data-driven recommendations regarding the possibility of re-initiation of dosing.

L2719: ## Additional Analyses Conducted on the Individual Trial
L2720: ## Correlation between Amyloid PET and Clinical Endpoints
L2721: The correlation between the change from baseline on amyloid PET and the change from baseline in clinical endpoints was explored separately in the placebo and donanemab treatment arms at the individual level. No statistically significant correlations were observed. It is not surprising that despite a treatment effect, there is not a tight correlation between reduction in brain A\beta plaque levels and clinical endpoints at the individual level. It has been recognized that brain A\beta burden is not well correlated with disease progression and there is not an a priori expectation of precisely how reduction in A\beta burden would relate to changes on clinical scales. Furthermore, when individual data from one dose level is used to quantify the relationship between two endpoints, it is challenging to correctly adjust the imbalances of multiple confounders due to potential nonlinear and complex relationships. Group-level correlation is not possible because only a single dose was included in the study.
L2722: Using a disease progression model, a decrease in amyloid plaque was associated with a slowing in disease progression relative to placebo. Similarly, a decrease in plasma p-tau 217 was also associated with a decrease in the rate of disease progression. See the clinical pharmacology review for a detailed review of these models.
L2723: ## 7. Integrated Review of Effectiveness
L2724: ## 7.1. Assessment of Efficacy Across Trials
L2725: This section is not applicable to this review because only one trial is reviewed.
L2726: ## 7.2. Additional Efficacy Considerations
L2727: ## 7.2.1. Considerations on Benefit in the Postmarket Setting
L2728: The population enrolled in Study AACG did not include patients at either end of the Alzheimer's disease continuum and there is some uncertainty with respect to the generalizability of benefit across the entire spectrum of Alzheimer's disease. There is a general expectation, however, that initiating treatment with donanemab earlier in the disease may provide the best opportunity to delay or halt the pathophysiological processes that lead to the clinical deficits of Alzheimer's disease. The ongoing study (Study AACM) of donanemab in individuals at risk for cognitive and functional decline of Alzheimer's disease should shed light on potential benefit in this population. Intervention with donanemab later in the disease may be expected to provide less benefit, as downstream pathological processes may dominate. The application does not contain clinical data to directly assess the effectiveness of donanemab at either end of the disease continuum. On the other hand, Alzheimer's disease is defined in part by the presence of amyloid pathology, and the pharmacodynamic effect of donanemab on reduction of brain amyloid plaque should occur across the disease continuum, providing the potential for clinical benefit.
L2729: Individuals with Down syndrome represent another important population at risk for Alzheimer's disease who might also benefit from treatment with donanemab. Alzheimer's disease in individuals with Down syndrome is likely driven by an overexpression of the gene for amyloid precursor protein located on chromosome 21, thus the pathology in this population is similar to that found in DIAD and sporadic Alzheimer's disease. One challenge is assessing changes in cognition and function in a population with intellectual disability. Also, people with Down syndrome have a higher incidence of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, which is associated with development of microhemorrhages. Additional safety data would be helpful to inform risk-benefit considerations in this population.
L2730: ## 7.3. Integrated Assessment of Effectiveness
L2731: The effect of donanemab on brain amyloid plaque demonstrated in Study AACG, an adequate and well-controlled study, was robust and persuasive and meets the statutory standard for substantial evidence of effectiveness to support accelerated approval. The proposed dosing regimen demonstrated a reduction in brain amyloid plaque from 107.2 Centiloids at baseline to
L2732: 23.1 Centiloids at Week 76 with a statistically significant difference from placebo of -85.1 Centiloids (p&lt;0.001). The magnitude of reduction is consistent with the observed reductions that supported the accelerated approvals of aducanumab and lecanemab.
L2733: The reduction of brain amyloid was highly persuasive. As observed in the placebo arm of Study AACG, amyloid plaque does not spontaneously disappear in patients with Alzheimer's disease. The reduction observed in the donanemab treatment arm is thus incompatible with variability or chance. Also, donanemab has demonstrated dose- and concentration-response relationships across doses in earlier single- and multiple ascending dose studies. The effects on amyloid are persuasive and consistent across subgroups, supporting the ability of Study AACG to be considered a single adequate and well-controlled trial that is capable of providing substantial evidence of effectiveness.
L2734: The clinical endpoint results from Study AACG provide context for the amyloid reduction observed in the study and inform the reasonable likelihood of the reduction in brain amyloid plaque to predict clinical benefit. Importantly, the prespecified primary endpoint in Study AACG was positive. Despite not reaching statistical significance according to the prespecified hierarchy, the estimates of the treatment effect at Week 76 across secondary clinical endpoints are consistent with a modest reduction of clinical decline. Importantly, a similar degree of reduction (approximately 20% to 40%) in the decline of clinical endpoints has been observed in other studies in which brain amyloid was reduced to a similar extent. This reduction corresponds to a delay in progression of several months over the 18 months of the study. Patients and caregivers have clearly expressed that a delay of several months at this stage of the disease is clinically important.
L2735: It is noted that the applicant did not require a formal clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia for enrollment in Study AACG. Instead, patients were enrolled based on Alzheimer's disease pathology and presence of clinical symptoms and objective evidence of cognitive impairment with scoring in the mild range. These criteria are generally consistent with an operationalization of the 2018 NIA-AA Research Framework for Alzheimer's disease (Jack et al. 2018) for mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease. Overall, the mean baseline scores on the CDR-SB, MMSE, ADAS-Cog 13, and the ADCS-iADL appear to be consistent with a study population with mild cognitive impairment and mild to minimal functional impairment, although there are a small number of outliers who had more marked impairment on these assessments. For this reason, it is appropriate for the indication statement to refer to mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease or mild Alzheimer's disease dementia.
L2736: The evidence provided in the submission clearly meets the criteria for accelerated approval. Alzheimer's disease is a serious and life-threatening condition with a tremendous unmet medical need. Donanemab targets the underlying pathology of the disease and may provide a
L2737: meaningful therapeutic benefit over existing treatment. Note that aducanumab and lecanemab have received accelerated approval and thus are not considered available treatment for this purpose. The Division has determined that an effect on brain amyloid plaque is reasonably likely to predict benefit. The data provided in the donanemab program and from topline results from other studies support this conclusion. Finally, donanemab has demonstrated a robust and statistically significant effect on reduction of brain amyloid plaque.

L2749: ## 12. Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L2750: In order to verify the clinical benefit of donanemab, the applicant will be required to conduct a randomized, controlled trial to evaluate the efficacy of donanemab compared to an appropriate
L2751: control for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease. The trial should be of a sufficient duration to observe changes on an acceptable endpoint in the patient population enrolled in the trial. The ongoing Study AACI is intended to address this requirement.

L2831: ## 5.2. Review Strategy
L2832: The clinical review of BLA 761248 is divided into a review of clinical efficacy (by Dr. Kevin Krudys) and this review of clinical safety. Information submitted as part of BLA 761248 and published literature are discussed in this review. I will primarily present analysis conducted by myself. The primary safety review presented here will focus on Study AACG to reflect the safety in the study that is the primary source of evidence of effectiveness. Studies AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort will provide supportive information.

L2846: AD: Alzheimer's disease, MCI: mild cognitive impairment
L2847: Study AACG, the proposed primary source for evidence of effectiveness, was the source for placebo-controlled safety analyses, and the results for this study are presented individually. The three open-label studies, AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort, were pooled with donanemab-treated participants from Study AACG to create an all-donanemab-treated pool, which allows for analysis of adverse events occurring with exposure to donanemab for up to 12 months.
L2848: Study AACG was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of donanemab in participants with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease and mild Alzheimer's dementia. The study was comprised of a 9-week screening period, an up to 72-week treatment period with final evaluations occurring 4 weeks later at Week 76, and a 48-week follow-up period. Participants were randomized to either donanemab 700 mg intravenously for the first three doses, then 1400 mg every four weeks for up to 72 weeks or to placebo intravenously every four weeks for up to 72 weeks.
L2849: In Study AACG, donanemab doses could be modified based on amyloid plaque reduction measured by florbetapir PET imaging or by the development of ARIA-E. Depending on the degree of amyloid plaque reduction noted at Week 24 or Week 52, donanemab doses could be reduced from 1400 mg to 700 mg or the participant could be switched to placebo. The reader is referred to the Appendix for further details on dose modifications related to ARIA in Study AACG.
L2850: The open-label studies differed from Study AACG in that the donanemab dose was not reduced to 700 mg based on amyloid plaque reduction criteria or the development of ARIA-E. In participants who met dose reduction criteria for amyloid plaque reduction, donanemab was discontinued. The reader is referred to the Appendix for further details on dose modifications related to ARIA in the open-label studies.
L2851: This submission also contains blinded safety data submitted by the sponsor for the ongoing placebo-controlled part of the main study of AACI. In the pre-BLA meeting package dated July 30, 2021, the sponsor proposed to unblind data from the placebo-controlled portion of Study AACI. In pre-BLA meeting minutes dated October 7, 2021, the Division noted that unblinding of data from a clinical trial would raise concerns about the impact on the study's integrity. In an
L2852: email communication dated March 4, 2022, the sponsor proposed to submit blinded data for the placebo-controlled period of Study AACI in response to the Division's communications.
L2853: ## Analysis of Adverse Events
L2854: The sponsor analyzed adverse events using two methods.
L2855: In the first analysis method, the sponsor included adverse events occurring on the date of the first dose of study drug through the date of the last dose of study drug + 57 days (where 57 days represents approximately five times the half-life of the drug). For participants randomized to the donanemab arm, the last dose of study drug is the last dose of donanemab.
L2856: *Reviewer comment: This method of analysis potentially introduces bias caused by observing AEs occurring in observation periods of unequal duration. Based on criteria outlined by study protocol as reasons for treatment discontinuation, participants experiencing adverse events such as ARIA and infusion reactions were more likely to discontinue treatment compared to participants who did not experience ARIA and infusion reactions, thus resulting in shorter periods of observation.*
L2857: In the second analysis method, adverse events were analyzed based on a treatment policy approach. In Study AACG, the sponsor included adverse events occurring within the 76-week placebo-controlled treatment period. In the open-label studies AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN Dona-Cohort, the sponsor included adverse events occurring during the treatment period (up to 76 weeks) and during the follow up period (up to 48 weeks).
L2858: *Reviewer comment: Analyses using this method results in comparison of adverse events occurring over equal lengths of observation within each study. In Study AACG, this method does not capture adverse events occurring in the follow-up period that are within five times the half-life of the last dose of donanemab.*
L2859: For the purpose of this review, adverse events were analyzed based on treatment period plus 57 days (~ 5 times the half-life of donanemab). In Study AACG, this method allows comparison of adverse events occurring in observations periods of similar duration in the active drug and placebo arms and includes AEs occurring within five times the half-life of the drug.
L2860: The sponsor analyzed safety results from Study AACD separately from the Phase 2 and 3 studies. Overall, the reviewer found this approach acceptable as participants in Study AACD had different dosing regimens.
L2861: Participants exposure to donanemab in Study AACD contributed towards the sponsor's calculations of 6- and 12-months donanemab exposures for the safety database. The reviewer
L2862: found this approach acceptable as doses at the 20 mg/kg weight approximated the proposed labeled dose.
L2863: Study AACC, a Phase 1 single and multiple-dose dose-escalation study, is not included among the key studies for this safety review as the maximum donanemab dose participants received was 10 mg/kg and is expected to result in lower exposures compared to exposures of participants in Phase 2 and 3 studies.
L2864: Amyloid related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) and hypersensitivity reactions are topics of special interest for the safety review of donanemab based on the safety profile of aducanumab, the first amyloid-directed monoclonal antibody drug, approved in June 2021 for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.1
L2865: Infusion related reactions and immunogenicity are also topics of special interest for this review, based on the observation of infusion related reactions occurring in Phase 1 studies with donanemab.

L2868: ## 8.2.1. Overall Exposure
L2869: Overall, the sponsor did not meet ICH guidelines of at least 100 patients exposed to the highest clinically relevant doses (700 mg every 4 weeks for 3 doses followed by 1400 mg every 4 weeks) for one year, but did meet ICH guidelines of at least 300 patients for six months. At the time of the 90-Day Safety Update, 49 participants were exposed for 12 months and 827 were exposed for 6 months. However, if considered using the protocol-designed approach (referred to as treatment policy approach) that allowed for reduction in dose or change to placebo based on amyloid plaque reduction, 100 patients were exposed for 12 months. Both approaches are considered in the sections that follow.
L2870: The primary safety data are from Study AACG, a completed placebo-controlled study. The dosing regimen in AACG provided for 700 mg q 4 weeks for 3 doses followed by 1400 mg q 4 weeks for up to 72 weeks, with an allowance for reduction to 700 mg or placebo based on amyloid plaque reduction at weeks 24 or 52 or based on the development of ARIA-E. Ongoing open-label studies AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort, with the same titration and that also include an allowance for stopping treatment based on amyloid plaque or development of ARIA-E, provide supportive information and were pooled with donanemab-treated subjects from Study AACG to create an all-donanemab pool allowing for analysis of adverse events occurring in patients who have had exposure for up to 12 months.

L2906: ## 8.2.2. Relevant characteristics of the safety population:
L2907: Overall, lower frequencies of female participants, participants of a minority race and ethnicity, and age over 85 years were observed in Study AACG compared to expected frequencies in the U.S. population with Alzheimer's disease. Baseline demographics were similar between donanemab and placebo arms in Study AACG. The safety profile of donanemab in patients with more advanced stages of AD is unknown. The population enrolled in the key studies for safety were identified as having MCI or mild AD, and treatment with donanemab was discontinued after achieving amyloid plaque reduction criteria.
L2908: The sponsor notes that participants were enrolled in Study AACG based on pathological staging
L2909: of Alzheimer's disease rather than phenotypic staging.2 Participants had to have both elevated amyloid measured by positron emission tomography (PET) and presence of tau pathology measured by flortuacipir PET in combination with a mini mental status exam score of 20 to 28. Participants also had to have gradual and progressive change in memory function reported by the participant or informant for \ge 6 months and be between 60 to 85 years of age.
L2910: *The reader is referred to the clinical review of efficacy by Dr. Kevin Krudys for an assessment of the adequacy of enrollment criteria used to identify patients with Alzheimer's disease and MCI or mild dementia in the clinical program.*
L2911: Participants were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: history of epilepsy or recurrent seizures; serious or unstable illness including cardiovascular, hepatic, renal, gastroenterologic, respiratory, endocrinologic, neurologic, psychiatric, immunologic, or hematologic condition; history of long QT syndrome; history of clinically significant multiple or severe drug allergies, or severe posttreatment hypersensitivity reactions; or had a centrally read MRI demonstrating presence of ARIA-E, &gt; 4 cerebral microhemorrhages, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, any intracerebral hemorrhage, or severe white matter disease. Participants were allowed to use approved medications for Alzheimer's disease concomitantly, if doses had been stable in the preceding two months before the first day of study drug administration. There were no exclusion criteria related to antithrombotics use in Study AACG.
L2912: Studies AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort had similar inclusion criteria related to change in memory and MMSE score as compared to AACG. Study AACN enrolled subjects between the age of 50 to 85 years of age inclusive.
L2913: Studies AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort had similar exclusion criteria as Study AACG including presence of ARIA-E, &gt; 4 cerebral microhemorrhages, more than 1 area of superficial siderosis, any intracerebral hemorrhage, or severe white matter disease at screening.
L2914: There were no exclusion criteria related to antithrombotic use in Studies AACH and AACI. In Study AACN, patients were excluded if they were on anticoagulants or antiplatelets (except for aspirin &lt; or = to 325 mg daily).
L2915: Participants were allowed to use approved medications for Alzheimer's disease concomitantly in the Phase 2 and 3 studies.
L2916: Baseline demographics were similar between the donanemab and placebo arms in Study AACG.

L2923: *According to the Alzheimer's Association 2022 Alzheimer's Disease and Facts and Figures, which contains U.S. data related to Alzheimer's disease, approximately two-thirds of Americans with Alzheimer's are women.3 In a population aged 65 years and older with Alzheimer's disease, 27% were between the ages of 65 to 74 years, 37% between 75 to 84 years, and 36% over 85 years. In the same report, studies on race and ethnicity in older populations demonstrate that compared to Whites, African Americans are twice as likely to have Alzheimer's dementia, and Hispanics are about 1.5 times as likely. Between 56 to 65% of people diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease have at least one copy of the ApoE \epsilon4 gene.*
L2924: A lower frequency of females was observed in the safety population of Study AACG compared to the frequency of females with Alzheimer's disease noted in the Alzheimer's Association 2022 report. The age range of 85 years and over was underrepresented in Study AACG compared to the frequency expected in the population as noted in the Alzheimer's Association 2022 report, likely because participants over the age of 85 years were excluded as per protocol. Blacks and Hispanics or Latinos were underrepresented in Study AACG compared to populations noted in the Alzheimer's Association 2022 report.
L2925: This reviewer did not note any significant differences in the baseline demographic characteristics by age, sex, or race in Study AACI Safety Addendum or AACN Dona-Cohort compared to Study AACG. Study AACN Dona-Cohort had a higher frequency of participants with mild cognitive impairment compared to Study AACG (34% versus 18%, respectively).
L2926: Baseline characteristics for the donanemab-BACE-I arm were similar to Study AACG overall, except for a higher frequency of participants with moderate Alzheimer's disease at baseline (27% versus 6%, respectively) and a lower frequency of memantine use at baseline (7% versus 23%, respectively).

L2929: ## *Reviewer comment:*
L2930: *The safety profile of donanemab in patients with more advanced stages of Alzheimer's dementia is unknown as patients enrolled in the key studies for safety were identified as having MCI or mild AD. Given that patients with moderate and severe dementia were not included in the studies, the safety outcomes from these studies potentially underestimate the impact of adverse events in patients with moderate or severe dementia given the increased likelihood of occurrence of other comorbid conditions with advanced dementia, including impaired memory, executive function decline, problems of gait and movement, malnutrition, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and falls.4*
L2931: *This reviewer notes that patients who continue treatment with donanemab after achieving amyloid plaque reduction criteria may develop more advanced stages of Alzheimer's disease, and safety outcomes in this population are unknown. In Study AACG, at Week 24 or Week 52 participants who met amyloid plaque reduction criteria had a dose reduction to donanemab 700 mg or to placebo based on the level of amyloid plaque reduction. In Studies AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort, participants who met amyloid plaque reduction criteria were switched to placebo during the study (Week 36 in AACH Part B, Weeks 24 and 52 in AACI Safety Addendum, and Weeks 24 and 52 in AACN-Dona Cohort).*
L2932: ## 8.2.3. Adequacy of the safety database:
L2933: 4 Feldman H and Woodward M. The staging and assessment of moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. AAN 2005; 65 (6 suppl 3). DOI: https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.65.6_suppl_3.S10
L2934: Overall, the low number of participants exposed to donanemab for 12 months or more at the proposed dose is low (n=49 at the time of the 90-Day Safety Update), and safety outcomes for this group are less certain than for participants with shorter durations of exposure. The sponsor and this reviewer used different methods to calculate exposure in the safety database. The sponsor's method of calculating exposure, based on a treatment policy approach, included participants who had dose reductions to 700 mg or were switched to placebo. Based on this approach, the sponsor calculated 877 participants with 6-months of exposure and 100 participants with 12-months of exposure in Studies AACG, AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN Dona Cohort. This reviewer based exposure calculations on participants exposed to donanemab at the proposed dose of 700 mg every four weeks for the first three doses, followed by 1400 mg every four weeks. With this approach, this reviewer calculated 827 participants with 6-months of exposure and 49 participants with 12-months of exposure in Studies AACG, AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, AACN Dona Cohort and AACD (including 7 participants from Study AACD exposed to doses at 20 mg/kg). The reviewer found this approach to be more appropriate as it includes participants exposed to donanemab at the proposed dose in labeling. According to the method of exposure calculation used by this reviewer, although the safety database meets ICH guidelines of at least 300 patients exposed for 6 months, it does not meet ICH guidelines of at least 100 patients exposed for one year. Overall, this reviewer found the number of participants exposed to donanemab for 12 months or more at the proposed dose to be low and the safety database as insufficient to adequately characterize the long-term safety of donanemab in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
L2935: The population studied was younger than U.S. populations with Alzheimer's disease and minority groups, including Blacks and Hispanics or Latinos, were underrepresented. The safety database consisted primarily of patients with mild cognitive impairment and mild Alzheimer's disease, which is the proposed target population.

L2946: ## 8.3.2. Categorization of Adverse Events
L2947: This reviewer notes that the method of recording AEs of ARIA-H in the adverse event datasets will likely underrepresent the frequency of ARIA-H experienced by participants in Studies AACG, AACH, and AACI. Data from MRIs may provide a better approximation of the frequency of ARIA-H. This reviewer considered the definitions for TEAEs and SAEs to be acceptable. In Study AACG, severity of AEs was based on the judgement of the principal investigator rather than on defined categories and could potentially result in inconsistent AE severity categorization among different principal investigators. *Translation of verbatim terms for adverse events to MedDRA preferred terms was adequate, except as noted below for events related to ARIA-H.*
L2948: The protocol for Study AACG specified that all adverse events occurring after signing of the
L2949: informed consent form were to be recorded in the case report form. Adverse events were collected at every visit, which occurred every four weeks during the treatment period and during visits in a 52-week follow-up period. The protocol specified that for adverse events that were serious, otherwise medically important, considered related to the investigational product or the study, or that caused the participant to discontinue the investigational product, the participant should be followed until the event resolves, stabilizes, or is reasonably explained. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined as events that first occurred or worsened after the randomization date (Visit 2, date of first infusion). Investigators recorded their assessment of the potential relatedness of each adverse event in the case report forms/electronic data entry. A serious adverse event (SAE) was defined as any AE that result in death, initial or prolonged inpatient hospitalization, a life-threatening experience, persistent or significant disability/incapacity, congenital anomaly/birth defect, or an important medical event that may not be immediately life-threatening or result in death or hospitalization but may jeopardize the patient or may require intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed above. In a response dated August 4, 2022, to an information request dated July 29, 2022, the sponsor noted that adverse events were coded to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 23.1, and then upcoded to version 24.1 for analyses for the integrated database.
L2950: The open-label studies provided accurate definitions of AEs and SAEs in their protocols. AEs were collected regardless of relatedness. Open-ended, non-leading verbal questions were used to detect adverse events. AEs were collected at each visit during treatment periods and during follow up periods that were at least five-times the half-life of the drug. Adverse events were assessed by events per participant. Adverse events were coded to Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 24.1.5
L2951: This reviewer noted that for USUBJID I5T-MC-AACG-[REDACTED](b) (6), the verbatim term of "asymptomatic severe ARIA-E with 2 microhemorrhages" was coded to the dictionary derived term "amyloid related imaging abnormality-edema/effusion" but not to "amyloid related imaging abnormality-microhemorrhages and hemosiderin deposits." In a response dated July 1, 2022, to an information request dated June 29, 2022, the sponsor noted that the protocols for Studies AACG, AACH, and AACI did not have dedicated case report forms to collect ARIA-H symptoms and that symptomatic ARIA-H was a notable event when serious or listed as a reason for discontinuation. The sponsor noted that the protocol in AACG did not require that ARIA-H be reported as an adverse event, and instead, it was captured as an MRI finding. The sponsor noted that MRI data is the more comprehensive and definitive source for identification of ARIA-H.

L2971: ## 8.4.1. Deaths
L2972: In the placebo-controlled study, a similar frequency of AEs with fatal outcome was observed between the donanemab and placebo arms (0.8% versus 1.6%, respectively). The frequency of AEs with fatal outcome in the all-donanemab pool did not exceed the frequency of AEs observed in the donanemab arm of the placebo-controlled trial. In a review of narratives submitted by the sponsor from Studies AACG, AACH Part B, AACI Safety Addendum, and AACN-Dona Cohort, this reviewer did not identify any deaths attributable to donanemab exposure. Twenty-two cases of AEs with fatal outcome were reported in the blinded main study of AACI at the time of the 90-Day Safety Update and one additional death from the blinded main study of AACI was subsequently reported after the 90-Day Safety Update. Three of the 23 blinded cases reported ARIA with fatal outcome. Although a role for donanemab could not be established in any of the 23 cases as the data were still blinded at the time of the submission, the three cases associated with ARIA and with fatal outcome are presumed to be related to donanemab for this safety assessment given the severity of ARIA and association of ARIA with amyloid-targeting monoclonal antibodies. Prescribing information will include the observation of fatal cases of ARIA. The contribution of donanemab and of ARIA to these deaths will be further explored when the ongoing trials are submitted.
L2973: In Study AACG, a total of two AEs with fatal outcome occurred in the donanemab arm and two in the placebo arm. The frequency of deaths by treatment policy was not higher in the donanemab arm compared to placebo with one death in the donanemab arm and two on
L2974: placebo (0.8% versus 1.6%, respectively). The fourth death occurred in the follow-up period. Preferred terms with fatal outcome in donanemab-treated participants were death and pneumonia. Preferred terms in placebo-treated participants were aspiration pneumonia and cardiac arrest.

In a review of the screening MRI and Study Day 71 MRI at a meeting dated September 9, 2022, Dr. Ranjit Mani assessed the cavernous malformation noted on the screening MRI as unlikely to have contributed to the bleed, given the difference in areas of the brain that were affected. The ingestion of acetylsalicylic acid prior to the event of ARIA-H may have also contributed to worsening of the outcome of the event.*

L3013: Taking into consideration the additional death in the all-donanemab pool at the time of the 90-Day Safety Update, the incidence of adverse events with fatal outcome was 0.4% (5/1304). The incidence of death at the time of the 90-Day Safety Update by person-years of exposure to donanemab-M or -C was 0.7% (7 deaths/1,000 person-years [5 deaths/709 person-years]).12 That does not exceed the reported incidence from Alzheimer's disease in the US of 133.8/1,000 person-years.13 This comparison is limited by comparing the population with early-stage Alzheimer's disease (mild cognitive impairment and mild dementia) with the overall Alzheimer's disease population inclusive of later stages.
